docs.title: Discover Available SYCL Devices
docs.text:
SYCL provides the sycl-ls utility for discovering available devices.

Run:

sycl-ls

[native_cpu:cpu][native_cpu:0] SYCL_NATIVE_CPU, SYCL Native CPU 0.1 [0.0.0]

Depending on the node, devices may include:

    CPU
    GPU
    NVIDIA CUDA device

For example, the environment may report a CPU device and an NVIDIA CUDA device.

This command is particularly useful before running a SYCL application because it verifies that the SYCL runtime can discover the required backend.

docs.title: Basic SYCL Program
docs.text:
Create a file:

cd /home/apps/softwares/sycl-stack/test

vim hello.cpp

Example SYCL program:

#include <sycl/sycl.hpp>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    sycl::queue q;

    std::cout << "Running on: "
                << q.get_device().get_info<sycl::info::device::name>()
                << "\n";

    q.single_task([]() {
        // SYCL kernel
    }).wait();

    std::cout << "Hello World from SYCL!\n";

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Compile a SYCL Program
docs.text:
The basic SYCL compilation command is:

clang++ -fsycl -fsycl-targets=native_cpu hello.cpp -o hello

Run:

./hello

    Running on: SYCL Native CPU
    Hello World from SYCL!

The default SYCL device selection depends on the available runtime and selector used by the application.

docs.title: CPU SYCL Compilation
docs.text:
For explicitly targeting the native CPU backend:

clang++ \
    -fsycl \
    -fsycl-targets=native_cpu \
    hello.cpp \
    -o hello_cpu

Run:

./hello_cpu

The executable will use the SYCL native CPU backend.

docs.title: Explicit CPU Device Selection
docs.text:
A program can explicitly select the CPU device.

Example:

#include <sycl/sycl.hpp>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    sycl::queue q(sycl::cpu_selector_v);

    auto device = q.get_device();

    std::cout << "CPU Device: "
                << device.get_info<
                        sycl::info::device::name>()
                << std::endl;

    q.parallel_for(
        sycl::range<1>(100),
        [=](sycl::id<1> i) {
            // CPU work
        }
    ).wait();

    return 0;
}

Compile:

clang++ \
    -fsycl \
    -fsycl-targets=native_cpu \
    hello_cpu.cpp \
    -o hello_cpu

Run:

./hello_cpu

CPU Device: SYCL Native CPU

docs.title: Example: Vector Addition
docs.text:
A simple SYCL vector addition program is useful for testing the environment.

#include <sycl/sycl.hpp>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const size_t N = 1000000;

    std::vector<float> A(N, 1.0f);
    std::vector<float> B(N, 2.0f);
    std::vector<float> C(N, 0.0f);

    sycl::queue q;

    float *d_A = sycl::malloc_device<float>(N, q);
    float *d_B = sycl::malloc_device<float>(N, q);
    float *d_C = sycl::malloc_device<float>(N, q);

    q.memcpy(d_A, A.data(), N * sizeof(float));
    q.memcpy(d_B, B.data(), N * sizeof(float));

    q.wait();

    q.parallel_for(
        sycl::range<1>(N),
        [=](sycl::id<1> i) {
            d_C[i] = d_A[i] + d_B[i];
        }
    ).wait();

    q.memcpy(C.data(), d_C, N * sizeof(float)).wait();

    std::cout << "C[0] = "
                << C[0]
                << std::endl;

    sycl::free(d_A, q);
    sycl::free(d_B, q);
    sycl::free(d_C, q);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: SYCL and MPI
docs.text:
SYCL provides parallelism inside a node.

MPI provides distributed-memory communication between processes and nodes.

Therefore, a multi-node application can use:

                MPI
                 |
       +---------+---------+
       |                   |
     Node 1              Node 2
       |                   |
     SYCL                 SYCL
       |                   |
    CPU/GPU             CPU/GPU

MPI handles communication between nodes while SYCL performs computation on the CPU or GPU available to each MPI process.

docs.title: MPI + SYCL Compilation
docs.text:
The custom MPICH installation provides:

mpicc
mpicxx
mpirun
mpiexec

For a C++ SYCL + MPI program:

mpicxx \
    -fsycl \
    program.cpp \
    -o program

For an NVIDIA GPU target:

mpicxx \
    -fsycl \
    -fsycl-targets=nvptx64-nvidia-cuda \
    program.cpp \
    -o program

docs.title: Simple MPI + SYCL Example
docs.text:
The following example calculates a local value using SYCL and then uses MPI to combine the results from all MPI ranks.

#include <sycl/sycl.hpp>
#include <mpi.h>

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);

    int rank;
    int size;

    MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &rank);
    MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &size);

    const int N = 1000000;

    sycl::queue q(sycl::cpu_selector_v);

    std::vector<int> data(N, 1);

    int *device_data =
        sycl::malloc_device<int>(N, q);

    q.memcpy(
        device_data,
        data.data(),
        N * sizeof(int)
    ).wait();

    int local_sum = 0;

    sycl::buffer<int> result_buf(
        &local_sum,
        sycl::range<1>(1)
    );

    q.submit([&](sycl::handler &h) {

        auto result =
            result_buf.get_access<
                sycl::access::mode::write>(h);

        h.parallel_for(
            sycl::range<1>(1),
            [=](sycl::id<1>) {

                int sum = 0;

                for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i)
                    sum += device_data[i];

                result[0] = sum;
            }
        );

    }).wait();

    int global_sum = 0;

    MPI_Reduce(
        &local_sum,
        &global_sum,
        1,
        MPI_INT,
        MPI_SUM,
        0,
        MPI_COMM_WORLD
    );

    if (rank == 0) {

        std::cout
            << "MPI ranks : "
            << size
            << std::endl;

        std::cout
            << "Global sum : "
            << global_sum
            << std::endl;
    }

    sycl::free(device_data, q);

    MPI_Finalize();

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Multi-Node GPU + MPI + SYCL
docs.text:
The same hybrid programming model can be extended to multiple GPU nodes.

Conceptually:

                 MPI
                  |
       +----------+----------+
       |                     |
     Node 1                Node 2
       |                     |
    MPI Rank 0             MPI Rank 1
       |                     |
     SYCL GPU              SYCL GPU
       |                     |
    NVIDIA GPU             NVIDIA GPU

Compile:

mpicxx \
    -fsycl \
    -fsycl-targets=nvptx64-nvidia-cuda \
    mpi_sycl.cpp \
    -o mpi_sycl_gpu

A corresponding SLURM job can request multiple nodes and one GPU per MPI process, depending on the GPU resource configuration of the cluster.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The 20 PF cluster provides a complete SYCL programming environment supporting CPU, NVIDIA GPU, MPI, and SLURM.

The environment can be loaded using:

module load sycl/cpu_gpu

or manually:

source /home/apps/softwares/sycl-stack/setup-env.sh

SYCL CPU compilation:

clang++ -fsycl \
    -fsycl-targets=native_cpu \
    program.cpp \
    -o program_cpu

SYCL NVIDIA GPU compilation:

clang++ -fsycl \
    -fsycl-targets=nvptx64-nvidia-cuda \
    program.cpp \
    -o program_gpu

MPI + SYCL compilation:

mpicxx -fsycl \
    -fsycl-targets=native_cpu \
    program.cpp \
    -o program

Multi-node applications are submitted through SLURM and launched using the installed MPICH runtime.

This provides a complete workflow for developing, compiling, testing, and executing heterogeneous SYCL applications on the 20 PF supercomputing infrastructure.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
GROMACS is a versatile package to perform molecular dynamics, i.e. simulate the Newtonian equations of motion for systems with hundreds to millions of particles, and is a community-driven project. It is primarily designed for biochemical molecules like proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids that have a lot of complicated bonded interactions, but since GROMACS is extremely fast at calculating the nonbonded interactions (that usually dominate simulations) many groups are also using it for research on non-biological systems, e.g. polymers and fluid dynamics.

Official site: https://www.gromacs.org/.

or

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name="rfm_job"
#SBATCH --ntasks=96
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=48
#SBATCH --output=rfm_job.out
#SBATCH --error=rfm_job.err
#SBATCH --exclusive
#SBATCH --partition=debug
#SBATCH --mem=180G



# 1. Initialize Spack
source /home/apps/spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh

# 2. Load ONLY OpenFOAM (Spack will load the correct MPI dependency automatically)
spack load openfoam/q5jbckq

# 3. Source the OpenFOAM environment to set correct PATH and MPI variables
source /home/apps/spack/opt/spack/linux-cascadelake/openfoam-2512-q5jbckqquhnhhyuzyysoiz4rdxlevonq/etc/bashrc
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1

# Extract the benchmark files
tar --strip-components 2 -xf Motorbike_bench_template.tar.gz bench_template/basecase

# Grant execute permissions
chmod +x Allclean Allmesh Allmesh_serial

# Clean previous run
./Allclean

# Patch for ESI OpenFOAM v2512 Compatibility
sed -i 's/surfaceFeatures/surfaceFeatureExtract/g' Allmesh
sed -i 's/surfaceFeatures/surfaceFeatureExtract/g' Allmesh_serial
if [ -f system/surfaceFeaturesDict ]; then
    mv system/surfaceFeaturesDict system/surfaceFeatureExtractDict
fi

# Configure decomposing and system files
sed -i -- "s/method .*/method          scotch;/g" system/decomposeParDict
sed -i -- "s/numberOfSubdomains .*/numberOfSubdomains 96;/g" system/decomposeParDict
sed -i -- 's/    #include "streamLines"//g' system/controlDict
sed -i -- 's/    #include "wallBoundedStreamLines"//g' system/controlDict
sed -i -- 's|caseDicts|caseDicts/mesh/generation|' system/meshQualityDict

# Execute meshing
./Allmesh

# Run using the correct mpirun configured by OpenFOAM
time \
mpirun -np 96 simpleFoam -parallel

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Bhaskera teaches a pre-trained language model something new, on a cluster of GPUs, from the command line. You give it three things: a model to start from, data to learn from, and one small file (a recipe) that says how. It does the rest: it checks that everything is in place, asks Slurm for the GPUs, starts the training across all of them, saves progress as it goes, and keeps a record of every run. It handles text models, and models that also read images, video and audio.

This is called fine-tuning. A model such as Qwen3 or Llama has learned general language from a huge amount of text. Fine-tuning continues its training on your own examples (your support tickets, your documents, your question and answer pairs) so that it answers the way you need. Bhaskera is for people who want to do that on a shared Slurm cluster without writing the distributed-training code themselves.

On PARAM Rudra it is tested from 1 node up to 128 nodes (256 A100 GPUs). Most runs use LoRA: the pre-trained model stays as it is and only a small add-on (an adapter) is trained, which needs far less GPU memory and far less communication between nodes. Full fine-tuning, which trains every weight, is available too.

Official site: https://github.com/kishoryd/Bhaskera. If you have never done this before, start with Start Here: Your First Run.

docs.title: What Bhaskera brings to the table
docs.text:
Fine-tuning a large model on a cluster is not one hard step but many small ones, and each can fail in its own way. Bhaskera is the work around the training, as well as the training itself.

You need to ... What Bhaskera does Describe a run One YAML file: the model, the data, how to spread the work over the GPUs. The same file runs on N nodes. Train at any size LoRA and QLoRA (4-bit) with DDP, FSDP2, HSDP and Pipeline parallelism, measured on PARAM Rudra with five models from 14 B to 235 B parameters, including mixture-of-experts models, on 8 to 128 nodes (Benchmarks). Full fine-tuning of every weight with DDP, FSDP2 or HSDP, tried on a 14 B model (Recipes). Train models that see and hear Images, video and audio (Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-Omni) with the same recipes and commands. Get your data in Tokenising from JSONL, JSON, CSV, TSV, Parquet, Arrow or plain text; models and datasets named by their Hugging Face address and downloaded for you, even from a login node that has no internet; datasets with names, versions and fingerprints, so every run records exactly what it trained on. Avoid wasting GPU hours Checks before anything is submitted: files and libraries are there, the model fits in GPU memory, the partition limits allow it, the disk has room for the checkpoints. A node that failed before is skipped. Survive failures Checkpoints, and resume to continue from the last one, or from an earlier one after a loss spike. A failed job ends with a plain explanation of what went wrong and on which node. Know whether it worked Benchmark the tuned model against its base on standard tests or on your own questions, see what tuning fixed and what it broke, compare models side by side, and chat with the result. Keep track Every run, its curves, its settings, its adapter and its GPU energy in MLflow, a model registry with names, versions and hand-off notes, and a web page for all of it. Use it on your cluster Everything that belongs to one cluster is a profile (partitions, GPUs, network), not code. See Setting Up on Another Cluster.

Two ways to use it: the command line (this guide's focus: ./submit.sh, a few small commands) and a web page that does the same things with buttons (Bhaskera Dashboard). Everything the page does can be done from a terminal.

docs.title: Pick your starting point
docs.text: Your situation Go to I have no model and no data. I want to see it work, or I will use a public model and dataset. Case 1 I bring my own model and my own data, tokenised or not. Case 2 I only want to measure a model I already have, with no training. Case 3 Version 1.0.0 (Python 3.11, PyTorch 2.6 with CUDA 12.4, transformers 4.57) Tested models Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.3-70B, Mistral-Large-123B (dense); Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-235B-A22B (MoE) Parallelism QLoRA + DDP (4-bit), DDP, Pipeline, FSDP, HSDP Multimodal Images, video and audio with Qwen3-VL and Qwen2.5-Omni (DDP, FSDP, HSDP) Partitions debug (tokenising), gpu-small, gpu-large, gpu-massive (training)

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
$ module load bhaskera/1.0.0
$ cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs     # your run folder: any folder you choose
$ cd /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs

$ ./submit.sh tokenize recipes/tokenize-chatml.yaml        # once: tokenise your data
$ ./submit.sh recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml 8 12             # recipe, nodes, hours
$ tail -f logs/qwen3-14b-qlora_<jobid>.out | grep --line-buffered -E '\[step|eval|exit code'

Note

If module avail bhaskera shows nothing, install your own copy as described in Installation; the rest of this guide is the same.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
All combinations of 5 models × 5 strategies × 5 node counts (8, 16, 32, 64, 128) were run on PARAM Rudra in November 2026:

How these numbers were measured

  • Each run trains for 10 steps with LoRA, then evaluates once on about 256 held-out conversations. Sequence length 4096, 2 × A100 80 GB per node.
  • Time to train is projected for one pass over a 1.24-billion-token training set from the measured speed over steps 3–10; startup (5–20 min) is excluded.
  • MFU is the share of the GPUs' peak bf16 maths speed spent on model work. For MoE models it counts only the active parameters.
  • Runs hit by a faulty GPU, node or network were rerun automatically; the tables show the successful attempt.
  • * At least one step of this run took more than 1.5× its median step time (a slow node or network hiccup). Slow steps are included in the numbers.
  • The training data was a 528,450-conversation ChatML instruction dataset (1.24 B real tokens); evaluation used a separate 3,000-conversation set.
