docs.title: What the results show
docs.text:
• QLoRA, DDP and Pipeline scale almost linearly: doubling the nodes nearly halves the time, and MFU stays flat from 8 to 128 nodes. Qwen3-14B with QLoRA goes from 12.5 h on 8 nodes to 49 min on 128 nodes.
  • For dense 70 B–123 B models, QLoRA + DDP is the fastest (37–39% MFU), followed by Pipeline (28–31%).
  • FSDP and HSDP are 3–4× slower and lose efficiency at 128 nodes (MFU 5–7%), because they move model weights over the network every step.
  • MoE models need the Pipeline strategy. With other strategies they run at 0.2–1.7% MFU.
  • Accuracy agrees across strategies. Within each model, eval accuracy differs by about one point or less between strategies and node counts, so the choice of strategy is about speed and memory, not quality.

docs.title: Data Format
docs.text: Tokenising reads your raw data in two steps of choice: the file type (how the rows are stored) and the column layout (data.format: what the columns mean). Plain text needs neither.

docs.title: 1. File type
docs.text:
Give train_path (and val_path) as a file, a folder, or a pattern such as /data/shards/*.csv. One path holds one file type (JSON lines and JSON arrays may mix); add .gz to any of them.

File type Notes JSONL .jsonl .ndjson The usual choice and the best for large data. The only type the data_tools helpers read. JSON .json One row per line, or one array [{...}]. An array is read whole into memory, so prefer JSONL when large. CSV / TSV .csv .tsv Header row; every cell is text. A cell holding a list as JSON text (messages, conversations) is decoded. Parquet .parquet, Arrow / Feather .arrow .feather Read as they are. Plain text .txt .text .md Documents with no columns: see Plain text. Hugging Face dataset on disk (save_to_disk folder) Point at one split's folder.

docs.title: 2. Column layout: data.format
docs.text:
data.format Each row needs Typical sources chatml messages: list of {role, content} OpenAI chat files, UltraChat, Nemotron alpaca instruction, output, optional input Alpaca sharegpt conversations: list of {from, value} ShareGPT, Vicuna, OpenHermes prompt_completion prompt, completion Q&A sets, OpenAI's older files dolly instruction, optional context, response Databricks Dolly qa question, answer, optional context SQuAD, TriviaQA scored_response prompt, response, score Rated or reward-scored answers tool_calling messages with tool_calls and tool turns, plus tools Glaive, xLAM, Hermes function calling reasoning messages with reasoning_content, or prompt + reasoning + answer OpenThoughts, DeepSeek-R1 distills

Other column names are set under data.format_options: messages_field, and <name>_field for the others (for example {prompt_field: question, completion_field: answer}).

Which to choose

A chat model: use a chat layout (chatml, sharegpt, tool_calling, reasoning), or add use_chat_template: true to dolly, qa or prompt_completion so the model's own chat template is used. Otherwise those three write plain labelled text (### Instruction:, Question: / Answer:).

Good to know

  • scored_response keeps only rows with score >= min_score (format_options: {min_score: 0.7}): fine-tuning on the good answers. It is not reward-model training or reinforcement learning; Bhaskera does neither.
  • tool_calling needs a model whose chat template supports tools (Qwen3, Llama 3.1+, Mistral and others). If tool schemas differ between rows, store tools as JSON text.
  • reasoning writes <think>…</think> before the answer (think_open / think_close change the markers). Reasoning is long: use a generous seq_len, since longer rows are cut.
  • No val_path: only the training data is tokenised and training runs without an evaluation set.

Verified on PARAM Rudra: the same 2,000 rows as CSV, TSV and a JSON array tokenised to identical caches; tool calling, prompt_completion and plain text went through a real tokenise run.

docs.title: Plain text
docs.text:
For books, code or articles, leave out data.format:

data:
  name: local
  train_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/books/      # a folder of .txt files
  val_path:   /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/val.txt
  seq_len: 4096
  format_options:
    text_split: file        # file | paragraphs | lines
    chunk: true
  • text_split sets what one example is: a whole file (default), a paragraph (blank-line separated) or a line.
  • chunk: true cuts each example into seq_len pieces ending in the end-of-text token. Without it a long example is cut after seq_len tokens, which for a book loses almost all of it.
  • One file is read by one worker, so split a very large file. Files are read as UTF-8. These two keys go in the recipe file; Create recipe does not ask for them.

docs.title: Data you tokenised yourself
docs.text:
A folder of Parquet files with input_ids and labels (and attention_mask, or set data.pack_sequences: true) works as data.tokenized_path, without Bhaskera's tokenise step. Rename columns with data.column_map. Write a metadata.json ({"model_name": "<model folder>", "seq_len": 4096}) next to the files: without it Bhaskera cannot check that the length and tokenizer match, and the dashboard does not list the folder. Rows are never re-padded, so data.seq_len must equal their length.

Getting data in from Hugging Face, and naming and versioning it: Downloads and Dataset Versions.

docs.title: Downloads and Dataset Versions
docs.text: This page covers getting data from Hugging Face (named in a recipe, from the terminal, or from the dashboard) and naming and versioning your data so you can say which data made which model. For what the data should look like, see Data Format.

docs.title: Name Hugging Face repositories in a recipe
docs.text:
model:
  name: Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B                  # a Hugging Face model
data:
  name: local
  format: alpaca
  train_path: hf://tatsu-lab/alpaca      # hf://owner/name@revision pins a version

./submit.sh downloads them first (on a machine with internet) into models/ and data/hf/ of your run folder, then runs a resolved copy of the recipe (.bhaskera/resolved/<recipe>.yaml). Your recipe is not changed and a finished download is not repeated. Train and validation (or test) parts are sorted into _splits/train and _splits/val, and val_path is filled in if you gave none. DRY_RUN=1 ./submit.sh ... only reports what would be downloaded.

docs.title: From the terminal
docs.text:
$ python -m bhaskera.downloads preview --kind model --repo Qwen/Qwen3-14B       # size, files, licence; downloads nothing
$ python -m bhaskera.downloads get --kind model --repo Qwen/Qwen3-14B --target /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-14B
$ python -m bhaskera.downloads get --kind dataset --repo tatsu-lab/alpaca --target /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/alpaca

Run get again to continue an interrupted download. A model that asks you to accept a licence (Llama, for example) needs a Hugging Face key: huggingface-cli login, or Sign in on the dashboard.

A login node with no internet

On PARAM Rudra only login01, login02, login03 and login05 reach the internet, and you cannot choose which node you land on. If yours cannot, get, preview, the dashboard and ./submit.sh run the work on one that can, over SSH, and say so (downloading on login01 ...). The nodes come from download_hosts in the cluster profile (or BHASKERA_DOWNLOAD_HOSTS, comma-separated). The target folder must be on the shared file system. A key set only as HF_TOKEN in your shell is not passed on: sign in once so the key is kept in a file every node can read. To work on login01 yourself, see Monitoring.

docs.title: From the dashboard
docs.text:
Open Downloads in the header, choose Download a model or Download a dataset, then:

  1. Type the repository as on huggingface.co (for example Qwen/Qwen3-14B); a revision is optional.
  2. Type a folder you can write to; it is created if missing.
  3. Check size shows the size, number of files, licence and whether access is gated. Nothing is downloaded yet.
  4. Download starts it, with a progress bar and Cancel. Starting it again continues where it stopped.

A finished model appears under Yours in the recipe form. A finished dataset is registered as a dataset version with its repository and revision as the source. Only Hugging Face is contacted, system folders are refused, a download above 50 GB asks you to confirm, free space is checked first, and one download runs at a time.

Signing in. Most models need no key. Private repositories and licence-gated models (Llama) do: create a read key at huggingface.co/settings/tokens, accept the licence on the model page, then paste the key under Hugging Face access in Downloads and press Sign in. It is kept in a file only you can read (<run folder>/.cache/huggingface/token), never shown again or written to a log or command line. Sign out deletes the file (an HF_TOKEN in the environment is not touched).

docs.title: Dataset versions
docs.text:
A dataset version is a name, a number and a fingerprint of the content, so you can say exactly which data made a model, even after the files were edited.

In Data on the Train page press Register data, give a name, and choose a tokenised cache or your raw data. Bhaskera reads the files once (in the background) and records the fingerprint, row count, size, source, an optional note and, for a tokenised cache, the sequence length and tokenizer.

  • Same content keeps its version; changed content becomes the next number (New version prefills the dialog). Old versions stay.
  • A version shows unchanged, changed or folder missing, checked without reading the files; Verify reads them and compares the fingerprint.
  • A run records its data version (dataset.name, dataset.version in MLflow), shown beside the run name.
  • Training on data that changed after registering is refused, naming the version, until you register it as a new version or restore the files. Data never registered is not affected.
  • Forget removes a version from the list; files are never touched. Runs made before this show no version.
$ python -m bhaskera.dataversions add --name support --path /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/train.jsonl --note "first cut"
$ python -m bhaskera.dataversions list
$ python -m bhaskera.dataversions verify support          # or support:2

The list is one small file, .bhaskera/datasets.json in your run folder; no server is needed.

docs.title: Bhaskera Dashboard: Train, Serve, Evaluate, Monitor
docs.text: bhaskera-dashboard ray serves one web page for everything you run. It lists your jobs and your recent runs, starts new jobs, and lets you talk to a model you have trained. It listens on the login node, is private to your user, and is opened from your laptop with the one SSH command described under Monitoring.

docs.title: Starting the page
docs.text:
From your laptop, in a terminal you leave open (bhaskera-dashboard ray --info prints the port; it is 20000 plus your user id modulo 10000):

$ ssh -p 4422 -L 8265:localhost:<port> <user>@paramrudra.cdacb.in \
    "bash -lc 'module load bhaskera/1.0.0 && cd /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs && bhaskera-dashboard ray'"

Then open http://localhost:8265. The command lands on whichever login node you are given; to start the page on a node of your choice, such as login01 (which has internet), see Land on a login node you choose. The page finds submit.sh in the folder you start it from (your run folder). If you start it from another folder, it uses ~/bhaskera-runs, which it makes from the shared kit the first time. Jobs are charged to your login name. module load is needed because a login shell started by ssh host "command" does not load it for you.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
The page has five pages, each with its own set of cards. The names across the top are links; point at a name to see a menu of what it holds, or click it to open the page. Clicking the Bhaskera logo returns to Home.

Page What is on it Home Four cards (a multimodal model, Chat, Benchmark, Save a model), your running jobs, and five numbers: running now, training runs, saved models, benchmarked, and the GPU energy used Train Create a recipe (text or multimodal model, prepare your own data, or a custom recipe), train from a recipe, resume a stopped run, your recent runs, and your registered data with its versions Serve Chat with a trained model, running chat servers, and every saved model Evaluate Benchmark one or several models, test your own questions, and compare models side by side Monitor MLflow, the Ray Dashboard while a job runs, cluster limits and node health

The New run button at the top right opens the same dialogs as the cards. Downloads in the header fetches a model or a dataset from Hugging Face into a folder you choose, and holds the Hugging Face sign-in (see Downloads and Dataset Versions). Docs lists the guides, including the Guide that explains the words used on the page. Your name at the top right opens the account menu, with the Guide and Log out. Log out asks first, then stops the page; jobs you already started keep running.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Jobs: state, partition, nodes and GPUs, progress and time left, and the live numbers from the job log (loss, evaluation loss and accuracy, MFU, tokens per second, step time, and the GPU energy used so far). The GPU load of each node is one click away. Buttons open the Ray Dashboard, the GPU charts, the log, and the run in MLflow.
  • Runs: your recent MLflow runs that Bhaskera made, including finished and failed ones. The table shows the latest 10; Show 10 more, Show all and Show fewer change that. Remove on a row takes a finished, failed or stalled run off the list, and Clear failed and stalled does that for all of them at once; both ask first. Removing only marks the run deleted in MLflow, so it can be brought back with mlflow runs restore --run-id <id>. Only your own Bhaskera runs can be removed, and never one that is still running. Runs that other tools wrote into the same MLflow store are not listed. A run that stopped writing is marked stalled. Runs that were benchmarked show the result, and runs that recorded GPU power show the GPU energy they used (see Monitoring).
  • Cluster limits and node health (on Monitor): your job slots in each partition, and any node a job found faulty. New jobs keep away from those nodes for three days.

docs.title: MLflow, the Ray Dashboard and Grafana
docs.text:
The Bhaskera dashboard is the one address for three tools that each answer a different question. All three are reached through the same tunnel (see Monitoring); you never open a second one.

Tool Answers Where on the dashboard Needs MLflow How did the run go? Loss and evaluation curves, throughput, GPU energy, every run compared, the model registry MLflow on Monitor, and MLflow run on each job Nothing extra: every run is recorded in ~/mlflow-runs and the dashboard starts MLflow itself Ray Dashboard Is every node of the job healthy right now? CPU, memory and GPU load per node, workers and their logs Ray Dashboard on Monitor and on each running job A running job; one link per job Grafana How did the GPUs and nodes behave over time? GPU, CPU and memory charts for every node GPU charts on Monitor and on each running job Prometheus and Grafana installed next to Bhaskera (the install step WITH_CHARTS); without them the node list still works and only the charts are missing

MLflow keeps its runs after a job ends; the Ray Dashboard and Grafana exist only while their job runs. Use MLflow to compare finished runs, and the Ray Dashboard and Grafana to find a slow or failing node in a running one.

docs.title: Starting things
docs.text:
Every card and menu entry opens one of these dialogs:

You choose What runs Create a recipe the model, the data, a method, how long writes recipes/<name>.yaml (nothing runs) Train a recipe, the number of nodes, optionally the hours ./submit.sh <recipe> <nodes> <hours> Resume a run that failed or was killed, and the step to continue from ./submit.sh resume --run <run id> Chat a trained run, or a registered model ./submit.sh serve --run <run id> Benchmark one or more trained runs, the tests ./submit.sh eval --run <run id> --tasks ... Register a trained run, a name, an optional alias and hand-off note python -m bhaskera.launcher.register add ... (no Slurm job: it takes a second)

Check first runs the partition limits and the recipe check and submits nothing. Start in the dialog submits (training and resuming ask once more before they use GPU hours). The page runs the same submit.sh you would run by hand, so every check still applies, and none can be skipped from the page. A recipe that still has <project>/<username> placeholders is listed but cannot be started. A recipe that uses HSDP or Pipeline is refused, with the reason, when its shard size or stages do not divide the GPUs of the nodes you chose.

docs.title: Create a recipe
docs.text:
A recipe is the saved list of choices for one training run: which model to teach, which examples to teach it with, and for how long. The page asks for what you know and fills in the rest.

  1. The model. A name for the recipe, text or multimodal (then also what the data holds: image, video, audio), and the method: QLoRA + DDP (the usual start for text models), DDP, FSDP2, HSDP, Pipeline, or Custom. QLoRA and Pipeline are text only, and the page does not offer them for multimodal models. The model is a Hugging Face folder that is already on disk.
  2. The data. Tokenised data already made is found by itself (in the folders your recipes point to and in cache next to submit.sh) and listed with its model, sequence length and number of rows. If you only have JSONL files, open My data is not tokenised yet, give the files, and press Prepare data: a short CPU job tokenises them once, and the result shows up in the list.
  3. The training. Steps, learning rate and LoRA rank are one click each; More options has batch size, gradient accumulation, how often to save a checkpoint, how often to evaluate and, for HSDP and Pipeline, the shard group size or the stages.

The recipe is checked with the training job's own loader before it is written, so it loads without warnings, and Check first shows the YAML without saving it. A recipe never overwrites an existing file. Training and resuming then work from the Train tab.

What to train. A small add-on (LoRA) is the default: the model stays as it is and a small add-on is trained on top, which needs far less memory and disk (QLoRA does the same on a model squeezed to 4 bits). The whole model (full fine-tune) trains every weight: it can learn more, but it needs far more GPU memory (every weight, its gradient and the optimizer state), so use FSDP2 or HSDP over several nodes, or DDP for a model that fits on one GPU. It uses a smaller learning rate (1e-5, set for you) and is not available with QLoRA or Pipeline. Its result stays in the checkpoints, so checkpoints cannot be switched off for it, and Chat, Benchmark and Register on the page, which need an adapter, are not offered for it yet.

Checkpoints (in The training): save them or not, how often (every N steps), how many to keep (the newest N; 0 keeps all), and the folder to save them in. A LoRA or QLoRA checkpoint holds only the trained add-on and its optimizer state: about 1 GB for a 14B model (measured: 449 MB and 493 MB). A full fine-tune checkpoint holds every weight and the optimizer state, about five times the size of the model (an estimate: around 140 GB for a 14B model), so keep few of those. Because home folders fill up fast, save checkpoints on a large disk (for example under /scratch): the recipe gets its own folder inside the one you give. Without a folder they go to checkpoints/ in your run folder. With checkpoints off, a run that stops cannot be resumed; it has to start again. Check first shows how much room the checkpoints have. A recipe whose checkpoints would not fit is refused.

All settings lists every option a recipe has (about 160), grouped as in the config file, searchable, each with what it does. Anything you type there wins over the choices above. A name that is not a recipe option is refused with the closest real name.

Custom is for people who already know the settings: paste or write a whole recipe as YAML, or load one of the starters shipped with Bhaskera (the files in configs/) or one of your recipes and edit it. A copy is saved under your name with its own run name and checkpoint folder, so it never writes over the original run's checkpoints. The Ray Dashboard host stays on the local machine whatever the YAML says.

docs.title: Chat with a trained model
docs.text:
Train with logging.mlflow_log_adapter: true so the adapter is stored with the run. Then press Chat on a finished run. A GPU node loads the base model and the adapter, which takes a few minutes. When it is ready, a chat window opens on the page:

  • Tuned answers with the fine-tuned model, Base with the original model, Compare shows both side by side. The base answer comes from the same weights with the adapter switched off, so nothing is loaded twice.
  • Options sets the creativity and the longest answer.

If the model reads images, video or audio (a multimodal run), the chat window has an Attach button: pick files, check the previews, and ask. The files stay in the conversation, so you can ask follow-up questions about them.

The Close server button in the chat window (or on the job's card) stops the server and frees its GPU node. It asks for a second click, so a stray click does nothing.

The server runs on the node, stops after two hours (SERVE_HOURS changes it) or when you cancel the job, and answers only you.

docs.title: Benchmark a trained model
docs.text:
Training loss says little about what the model can still do. Benchmark runs standard tests (lm-evaluation-harness: ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, GSM8K and more) on the base model and on the tuned model, and shows the change per task. A change counts as better or worse only when it is larger than twice the standard error; otherwise it reads "no clear change". The result is stored with the training run and shown in the Runs table.

Compute nodes have no internet, so download the test data once on a login node:

$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate prepare --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag

From the terminal: ./submit.sh eval --run <run id> --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag --limit 200 (--limit uses 200 examples per task for a quick check; leave it out for the real score).

On the page you can tick several models (your runs, or registered names such as my-assistant:2): each gets its own job. More options sets how many examples are shown in each question (few-shot) and can skip the base model when you only need the tuned score. Your own tests (below) are ticked next to the standard ones.

docs.title: Compare models
docs.text: Once runs have been benchmarked, Compare models appears under the Runs table. Tick the models to put side by side: for each test, every model's score, with the score of the base model it started from in brackets, and the best in each row in bold. Use the same tests and the same number of examples for every model, and note that models with different base models are comparable only on the same test.

docs.title: The same things from the terminal
docs.text:
Everything the page does is also a plain command, so you can use either, or both, on the same jobs.

What On the page In the terminal Train a model New run, Train ./submit.sh recipes/<recipe>.yaml <nodes> <hours> Check without submitting Check first DRY_RUN=1 ./submit.sh recipes/<recipe>.yaml <nodes> <hours> Chat with a trained model Chat on a run ./submit.sh serve --run <run id>, then the steps below Benchmark a trained model Benchmark on a run ./submit.sh eval --run <run id> --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag --limit 200 --save-samples Watch a job the job card and Logs squeue -u $USER and tail -f logs/<name>_<job>.out Make a recipe New run, Create recipe write recipes/<name>.yaml (see Recipes) Save a trained model under a name Register python -m bhaskera.launcher.register add --run <run id> --name <model> --alias champion (see Model Registry) Continue a run that stopped Resume on the run ./submit.sh resume --run <run id> (see Resuming a Job) Stop a job Cancel job on its card (two clicks); Close server for a chat server scancel <job> Look at runs and curves the Runs table, MLflow bhaskera-dashboard start

docs.title: Chat from the terminal
docs.text:
./submit.sh serve --run <run id>                 # prints the job number
tail -f logs/bhaskera-serve_<job>.out            # wait for: === serving on <node>:<port> ===
ssh -N -L <port>:localhost:<port> <node> &       # on the login node: a link to the model
curl -s localhost:<port>/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is HPC?"}], "max_tokens": 200}'

The answer is in choices[0].message.content of the reply. Add "use_adapter": false to get the base model's answer from the same weights. The server answers only you and stops after the hours you gave (SERVE_HOURS, default 2) or with scancel <job>. On the page you skip all of this: the chat window opens by itself when the model is loaded.

docs.title: Test the model on your own questions, and find what to correct
docs.text:
The standard benchmarks say little about your own use. Test the model on examples from your own work:

  1. Put them in a JSONL file on /scratch, one per line: {"question": "...", "answer": "..."}.
  2. Turn the file into a test (it goes into a tasks folder next to submit.sh, which Bhaskera picks up by itself): python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate init-task --name my_test --data /scratch/<project>/<username>/my.jsonl
  3. Run it. On the page, open Benchmark, then Add a test of your own (the file, the names of the question and answer fields): it runs the command above for you and ticks the test. In the terminal: ./submit.sh eval --run <run id> --tasks my_test --save-samples
  4. Review the mistakes: python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate review <folder>. It sorts every example into fixed by tuning, broken by tuning (the base model had it right), still wrong and still right, prints a few of each, and writes review_my_test.jsonl with the prompt, the expected answer and both models' responses. The same files are stored with the training run in MLflow, under lm_eval/samples.
  5. Correct the data. Still wrong usually means examples are missing or wrong in your training data; broken means the tuning was too narrow or ran too long. Fix or add examples, tokenise again, train again, and run the same test: the numbers show whether it helped.

The model is asked Question: ... Answer:, and the test passes an example when the first line of its reply contains the expected answer, ignoring case and punctuation. For answers that can be worded many ways, change metric_list in the generated file (the lm-evaluation-harness documents the options), or write the test as multiple choice. During training, logging.mlflow_eval_samples: <n> also stores example predictions on your validation split at every evaluation.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: The Models section (on the Serve page) lists every registered model version: the model, its version, the run it came from, its aliases and its evaluation loss, with Chat and Benchmark buttons. Only versions that Bhaskera registered are listed. It is read from the registry directly, so it works with no job running and does not need MLflow's own page. A pencil next to the name means a hand-off note is kept with the version; hover over the row to read it. See Saving and Finding Your Models.

docs.title: What "job slots" means
docs.text:
The page shows, for example, 0 of 4 job slots used in gpu-debug. This is a cluster rule, not a Bhaskera setting: the batch system allows each user a fixed number of jobs submitted at once in a partition (on PARAM Rudra, gpu-debug allows 4 submitted and 2 running, at most 1 hour each). Bhaskera reads the limit from Slurm, shows how much of it you use, and checks it before submitting, so a job that would be refused is stopped with a clear message. On an account that several people share, everyone's jobs count together.

Shared accounts

The page lists the jobs of the Unix account you are logged in with. On an account that several people share, you see everyone's jobs, and anyone on it can start jobs from the page.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: There are two ways to use Bhaskera on PARAM Rudra. Most users should load the module.

docs.title: Option A: Module (recommended)
docs.text:
$ module avail bhaskera
$ module load bhaskera/1.0.0

The module provides:

Item Where Commands bhaskera-tokenize, bhaskera-train, bhaskera-dashboard and the Python environment on PATH Job scripts (submit.sh, train.sbatch, tokenize.sbatch, eval.sbatch, serve.sbatch), tested recipes and the PARAM Rudra cluster profile $BHASKERA_KIT Bhaskera source $BHASKERA_DIR

Copy the job scripts and recipes into your own folder on /scratch:

$ cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs
$ cd /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs
$ ls
clusters  eval.sbatch  recipes  serve.sbatch  submit.sh  tokenize.sbatch  train.sbatch

Continue with the End-to-end Example.

docs.title: Option B: Your Own Installation
docs.text:
Install once from a login node into your /scratch area (5 to 15 minutes, depending on file-system load). Use this if the module is not available, or if you want to change Bhaskera's code.

$ cd /scratch/<project>/<username>
$ git clone https://github.com/kishoryd/Bhaskera.git
$ cd Bhaskera
$ BHASKERA_CUDA=12.4 bash setup.sh
$ source .venv/bin/activate
$ uv pip install "https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/releases/download/v2.7.3/flash_attn-2.7.3+cu12torch2.6cxx11abiFALSE-cp311-cp311-linux_x86_64.whl"
$ uv pip install -r slurm/requirements-paramrudra.lock

Why each step is needed

  • BHASKERA_CUDA=12.4: login nodes have no GPU. Without it, setup.sh finds no CUDA and installs a CPU-only PyTorch that cannot train.
  • Prebuilt flash-attention: setup.sh tries to compile flash-attention, which needs the CUDA compiler (nvcc); there is no CUDA 12 compiler module on PARAM Rudra, so that step fails. The prebuilt package needs no compiler. All recipes need flash-attention (sequence packing uses it).
  • requirements-paramrudra.lock: the exact package versions used for every benchmark run. With newer Ray and grpcio releases, multi-node jobs fail at start-up (InvalidAuthToken, or the worker nodes time out waiting for the first node).

Then tell the job scripts where Bhaskera is, and copy the job scripts and recipes:

$ export BHASKERA_DIR=/scratch/<project>/<username>/Bhaskera      # add this line to ~/.bashrc
$ cp -r $BHASKERA_DIR/slurm /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
$ python -c "import torch, flash_attn, bitsandbytes, bhaskera; print('OK', torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda)"
OK 2.6.0+cu124 12.4

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A Bhaskera job can be followed in three places:

Where What it shows Best for The job log One line per step, and a one-line summary of all nodes every 10 steps A quick look while the job runs MLflow Training curves, and GPU and host curves for the whole job and for each node Comparing runs, and looking back at a finished run Ray Dashboard Every node of the running job with its CPU, memory and GPU load, and the logs of each worker Looking at the nodes while the job runs, at any number of nodes

docs.title: The Step Log
docs.text:
Every training step prints one line to the job log. Follow it while the job runs:

$ squeue -u $USER
$ tail -f logs/<recipe>_<jobid>.out | grep --line-buffered -E '\[step|eval|exit code'

Two steps and the evaluation from a Qwen3-14B QLoRA run on 8 nodes:

[epoch 0][step 9] loss=1.1703 lr=1.81e-05 grad_norm=0.2473 tok/s=27711 MFU=35.8% HFU=53.2% pad=0% step_s=4.70 MFU_step=36.0% mem=16.0/16.3GiB
[epoch 0][step 10] loss=1.0350 lr=2.01e-05 grad_norm=0.2650 tok/s=27620 MFU=35.7% HFU=53.0% pad=0% step_s=4.81 MFU_step=35.2% mem=16.0/16.3GiB
[epoch 0][step 10] eval_loss=1.5705 eval_acc=0.6557
Field Meaning loss Training loss (lower is better) eval_loss, eval_acc Loss and next-token accuracy on your validation data lr, grad_norm Learning rate; size of the update (a sudden jump is a warning sign) tok/s Real (non-padding) tokens processed per second by all GPUs together MFU Share of the GPUs' peak maths speed doing useful model work pad Share of each batch that is padding (about 0% with sequence packing) step_s Seconds for this step mem Peak GPU memory on the busiest GPU of the job, allocated / reserved slowest=rN Shown when one GPU lags: the slowest rank, and its step time against the median

Every 10 steps a second line summarises all nodes of the job:

[step 30] nodes=5 gpus=10 gpu_util=94/98/99% (min/mean/max) gpu_mem_max=17.7GiB temp_max=58C

A low minimum next to a high mean points at one GPU that is waiting for the others. The interval is monitoring.metrics.node_stats_every_n_steps in the recipe (0 turns the summary and the node curves off).

Check the log, not only the job state

A job can end as COMPLETED in SLURM even when training failed. A successful run ends with === training exit code: 0 ===.

docs.title: GPU energy used
docs.text:
Every run records the power its GPUs draw (summed over all the GPUs of the job, every ten steps). Bhaskera works out the energy from that curve: the area under it, in kWh. It shows on the Bhaskera Dashboard as GPU energy used (a total), as a GPU energy column in the runs table, and as GPU energy so far on a job that is running. The figure is the sum, over the readings, of the time between two readings multiplied by the average of the two power values.

  • It counts the GPUs only. CPUs, memory, fans, cooling and the network are not included, so the node's real use is higher.
  • It covers the time between the first and the last power reading, which is the training itself (not the minutes the model takes to load).
  • A run made with an older Bhaskera has no figure and shows a dash, because the default metric level used to drop the power reading. Nothing is estimated for it.
  • It is a measurement of what a run used. It is not a comparison with another method or another tool.

docs.title: MLflow Dashboard
docs.text:
Every run is recorded with MLflow under ~/mlflow-runs, so runs can be charted and compared in a web page. The Ray Dashboard command below starts MLflow for you. To run MLflow on its own, start it on a login node:

$ module load bhaskera/1.0.0
$ bhaskera-dashboard start --port 5055      # the port is remembered for next time
$ bhaskera-dashboard status
$ bhaskera-dashboard tunnel                 # prints the SSH command for your laptop

bhaskera-dashboard tunnel prints the command for the login node you are on. Run it on your laptop and leave that terminal open:

  From your laptop (leave it open):
    ssh -p 4422 -t -t -L 5055:localhost:15055 <user>@paramrudra.cdacb.in "ssh -t -t -L 15055:localhost:5055 login01"
    then open http://localhost:5055

The command has two hops because paramrudra.cdacb.in hands out a different login node each time you connect (login01, login03, login05 and so on), and MLflow runs only on the node where you started it. The first ssh logs in, and the second one, inside it, goes on to the node that runs MLflow (login01 here; the command always names the node you started it on). Then open http://localhost:5055 and choose the experiment bhaskera.

Do not use ssh -J

ssh -J <user>@paramrudra.cdacb.in:4422 <user>@login01 does not work: the login nodes refuse to pass a connection on to another machine. Use the two-hop command above.

MLflow stops when you log out

The MLflow started by bhaskera-dashboard start ends when the login session that started it ends (checked on PARAM Rudra: started over a one-line ssh, it was gone afterwards). Keep a session open for as long as you look at the charts: the tunnel command above leaves you in a shell on that node, so the simplest way is to run bhaskera-dashboard start in that shell, in a second terminal opened with the same ssh ... login01 hop, or to use the dashboard (bhaskera-dashboard ray), which starts MLflow itself and keeps it while the page runs.

Closing it

Press Ctrl-C in the laptop terminal, or type exit. The tunnel closes. Run bhaskera-dashboard stop on the login node if MLflow is still running.

A multi-node job is one run. It has these curves:

Metric What it is loss, lr, grad_norm, eval_loss, eval_accuracy The model throughput_tokens_per_sec, throughput_mfu_pct Speed of the whole job time_step_max_s, time_step_median_s, time_slowest_rank Spread of the step time over all ranks: the straggler signal cluster_gpu_util_pct_min, _mean, _max GPU utilisation over every GPU of every node cluster_gpu_mem_used_gib_max, cluster_gpu_temp_c_max, cluster_gpu_power_w_sum Memory, temperature and power over every GPU node_<host>_gpu<i>_util_pct, _mem_used_gib, _temp_c, _power_w One set of curves per GPU of each node, for example node_cbgpu0241_gpu0_util_pct node_<host>_cpu_pct, _mem_used_pct, _loadavg_1m CPU and memory of each node

MLflow shows the / of a metric name as _. Type cluster or a node name in the metric filter to find these curves. The older gpu_0_..., gpu_1_... and sys_... curves describe only the node of rank 0.

The node_<host>_... curves are written while the job has at most 16 nodes (monitoring.metrics.node_stats_per_node_max). A larger job would write more than a thousand curves every time, so it keeps the cluster_... curves, and the Ray Dashboard shows the individual nodes.

Stop the MLflow dashboard when you are done:

$ bhaskera-dashboard stop

Note

The MLflow dashboard runs only on the login node where you started it, so the tunnel must end on that login node. If the port is in use, choose another with --port.

docs.title: Ray Dashboard, Charts and MLflow in One Place
docs.text:
Ray starts a dashboard on the first node of every job, and every job has its own. Each lists all nodes of the job with their CPU, memory and GPU load, with charts over time, and works for any number of nodes. These dashboards listen on their node only, so they are reached through an SSH tunnel. You do not need to know which node a job runs on, or wait for it to start: bhaskera-dashboard ray finds your running jobs, links each of them, and puts everything behind one address.

$ module load bhaskera/1.0.0
$ bhaskera-dashboard ray                  # or: bhaskera-dashboard ray --job <jobid>

From your laptop, this one command logs in and keeps everything open
(the command is always the same; it finds your jobs and their nodes by itself):

    ssh -p 4422 -L 8265:localhost:20029 <user>@paramrudra.cdacb.in "bash -lc 'module load bhaskera/1.0.0 && bhaskera-dashboard ray'"

Then open http://localhost:8265 in a browser: your running jobs, with their Ray Dashboards,
charts and MLflow, are linked from that page.

The port in the command (20029 here) is your own: bhaskera-dashboard ray --info prints the command with the right one.

docs.title: Land on a login node you choose (login01 has internet)
docs.text:
The command above starts the page on whichever login node you are given. That is fine for everything except downloads from Hugging Face, which need internet, and on PARAM Rudra only login01, login02, login03 and login05 have it. (The page already sends a download to a node that has internet when it runs on one that does not, so this is only needed if you want to be on login01 yourself.) To start the page on a given node, add --node:

$ bhaskera-dashboard ray --info --node login01
    ssh -p 4422 -t -t -L 8265:localhost:18265 <user>@paramrudra.cdacb.in "ssh -t -t -L 18265:localhost:20029 login01 \"bash -lc 'module load bhaskera/1.0.0 && bhaskera-dashboard ray'\""

Run the printed line on your laptop, as it is printed, and open http://localhost:8265. Only one copy of the page can run per user on a node: if it says the port is in use, stop the old one (Ctrl-C in its terminal).

If the connection hangs: \"timed out during banner exchange\"

The login nodes slow down when many connections arrive in a short time (several ssh and scp commands in a row, for example). Wait a minute and try again, and open one connection at a time. Nothing is wrong with your account.

The same page starts jobs

The page also starts jobs, opens a chat with a trained model and runs benchmarks: see Bhaskera Dashboard.

Run that command on your laptop, leave it open, and open http://localhost:8265. That page lists your running jobs, and for each one a link to its Ray Dashboard and its Grafana charts, and a link to MLflow. Run the command before or after you submit a job. Jobs that start later appear on the page by themselves, and a job that ends is removed. The number after -L on the login-node side is reserved for your user name, so it differs from user to user and stays the same for you.

To avoid typing the command, run bhaskera-dashboard ssh-config on the login node and paste the block it prints into ~/.ssh/config on your laptop (once). From then on:

$ ssh bhaskera-ray

Laptops

The ssh-config entry needs OpenSSH 7.6 or newer, which Mac, Linux and Windows 10 or later have. With PuTTY, or if port 8265 is already in use on your laptop, forward the port from VS Code (below). The links on the page look like http://job-<id>.localhost:8265; Chrome, Edge and Firefox send such names to your own computer without any setup.

In the Ray Dashboard of a job:

  • Cluster lists every node with its CPU, memory and, per GPU, utilisation and memory. A node that is idle or full stands out here.
  • Cluster utilization (on the Overview page) and Metrics draw GPU, CPU and memory over time for every node. They are Grafana charts, also reached from the page under Grafana charts. They are there when Prometheus and Grafana are installed next to Bhaskera (the module sets BHASKERA_OBSERVABILITY); the job log says charts: Prometheus and Grafana started when they run. Without them the node list still works, only the charts are missing.
  • Jobs shows the training job and its workers; Logs has the output of each worker, which helps when one node fails.

Two entries for one job

Ray numbers its jobs itself (01000000, 02000000), so these numbers differ from the SLURM job ID. One SLURM job shows two entries. The first is ray symmetric-run, which starts the cluster on every node and has no tasks. The second is the training itself.

After the job ends or fails

The Ray Dashboard and the charts exist only while the job runs. The command starts MLflow on the login node for you and keeps the connection open when a job ends, so the metrics stay under MLflow on the page. A run that stopped with an error is marked FAILED and keeps the curves logged up to that point. A run whose job was killed (time limit, failed node) is marked KILLED the next time the command runs.

Use --job <jobid> to show one job only, or any running job that was not started with submit.sh.

VS Code

If you work through VS Code Remote-SSH, run bhaskera-dashboard ray in its terminal, then forward port 8265 from the Ports tab instead of typing the tunnel command.

docs.title: Multimodal Fine-tuning
docs.text:
Bhaskera also fine-tunes models that read images, video and audio next to text, with the same strategies, recipes and cluster setup as text models. The output is text.

Input Model family Tested with Image Qwen3-VL (2B to 32B) Qwen3-VL-2B and 8B Video Qwen3-VL (same model) Qwen3-VL-2B Audio Qwen2.5-Omni (thinker) Qwen2.5-Omni-3B

Supported strategies: DDP, FSDP2 and HSDP. The Pipeline strategy, QLoRA and sequence packing are not available for these models; the run is refused before it starts, with the reason.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
One JSON object per line. content is a list of parts, also for plain text:

{"messages": [
  {"role": "user", "content": [
    {"type": "image", "image": "/scratch/<project>/<username>/data/pokemon/00001.png"},
    {"type": "text",  "text": "Describe this Pokemon in one short sentence."}]},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "a green dragon with wings"}]}]}

{"type": "video", "video": path} and {"type": "audio", "audio": path} work the same way. Images, video and audio stay on disk; only their paths and token counts are cached, and they are decoded while training.

docs.title: Chat with images, video and audio
docs.text: Once a multimodal run has finished with its adapter stored, Chat on the dashboard starts a server that reads files too, and the chat window gets an Attach button. Over the API, a message's content can be a list of parts (text, image, video, audio, with the files as base64). Files are checked by their own content and size before the model sees them.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Start from the multimodal starters in configs/multimodal/ of your run folder (a run folder made before this was added needs cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT/configs .): one for DDP, FSDP2 and HSDP, and a tokenizer config for vision (tokenize_vision.yaml, image and video) and one for audio (tokenize_audio.yaml).

$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.tokenize --config configs/multimodal/tokenize_vision.yaml --split both
$ ./submit.sh configs/multimodal/fsdp.yaml <nodes> <hours>

Put the two printed cache paths into the training config first. Important settings: data.modalities (any of text, image, video, audio), data.image_max_pixels (about 1 million pixels is at most 1024 visual tokens per image) and model.freeze_encoders (the vision and audio towers are frozen by default). Every setting, and how the encoders are split across GPUs, is in the guide in the repository: docs/multimodal/README.md.

docs.title: Full Configs
docs.text: The multimodal starters are shown in full under Recipes.

docs.title: Setting Up Bhaskera on Another Cluster
docs.text:
This page is for the person who installs Bhaskera on a cluster for the first time: an administrator, or an engineer with a few Slurm GPU nodes. It takes about an hour, most of it waiting for downloads. The other pages of this guide describe PARAM Rudra, where Bhaskera has been built and tested. Everything that is specific to a cluster lives in two places you will edit (a cluster profile and a modulefile), so no code needs to change.

What has been tested

Bhaskera has been run end to end only on PARAM Rudra: A100 80 GB GPUs, 2 GPUs per node, InfiniBand, Slurm, Lmod, and compute nodes without internet. On any other cluster, treat your first job as a test and follow the check at the end of this page before you tell users it works. GPUs other than the A100 80 GB, CPUs other than x86-64, and CUDA versions other than 12.x have not been tried.

docs.title: What your cluster needs
docs.text:
Need Why Check Slurm with GPUs requested as --gres=gpu:N Every job goes through sbatch sinfo -o '%P %G %l' lists a GPU partition NVIDIA GPUs and a driver that supports CUDA 12.4 The installed PyTorch is built for CUDA 12.4 nvidia-smi on a GPU node Linux on x86-64 The prebuilt flash-attention package is for it uname -m prints x86_64 A shared file system that the login nodes and all compute nodes see at the same path The install, recipes, data and checkpoints are read by every node The same ls on a login node and in a job A login node with internet (compute nodes do not need it) The installer downloads Python packages and flash-attention; models and datasets are downloaded there too curl -sI https://pypi.org git and about 15 GB free for the install The install is about 8 GB (the Python environment with PyTorch is most of it), plus room to update df -h <install folder> Permission to give users read access to the install folder One central install serves everyone You can write the folder and chmod a+rX it

Helpful but optional: Lmod or Environment Modules (users then run module load bhaskera), sacctmgr (so the page can show each user's job limits), and a place to keep shared models and data. Compute nodes without internet are fine, and are the usual case: Bhaskera switches Hugging Face to offline mode inside jobs.

docs.title: Decide these first
docs.text:
You will write these down once, in the cluster profile.

Decision How to find it Where to install, for example /apps/bhaskera/1.0.0 A path that users and compute nodes can read. The environment is built there and cannot be moved afterwards GPUs per node scontrol show node <gpu node> | grep Gres Memory of one GPU, in GB nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total --format=csv CPUs and memory to ask for on each node scontrol show node <gpu node>. Many sites give GPU jobs a small memory default, so name a number The fast network interface ip -4 addr on a compute node: the InfiniBand or high-speed Ethernet name (ib0, eth1, ...). Leave it empty to skip the setting Partitions, from the smallest jobs to the largest, with their time limits sinfo -o '%P %D %l' and your site's policy on how many nodes each partition takes

docs.title: Step 1: Install
docs.text:
Run this once, on a login node, as the person who owns the install folder. Use a checkout of the version you want:

$ git clone https://github.com/kishoryd/Bhaskera.git && cd Bhaskera
$ REF=main PREFIX=/apps/bhaskera/1.0.0 bash slurm/install-bhaskera.sh

REF is the version to install (a tag, branch or commit). The script's default is the tag v1.0.0, which was made before the newest features; use REF=main, or a newer tag, to get the page described in this guide. PREFIX is the install folder. WITH_CHARTS=0 skips Prometheus and Grafana (the time-series charts of the Ray Dashboard; the dashboard still lists nodes and GPUs without them), and WITH_EVAL=0 skips the benchmark package.

The script makes, under PREFIX:

Folder What it holds src/ The Bhaskera source, at REF python/, venv/ A Python 3.11 interpreter and an environment with PyTorch 2.6 (CUDA 12.4), flash-attention 2.7.3, bitsandbytes, Ray, PEFT and the pinned versions below observability/ Prometheus and Grafana, unless skipped share/kit/ The job scripts (submit.sh, *.sbatch), ready recipes, the text and multimodal starter configs (configs/) and cluster profiles, which users copy

Why the versions are pinned

slurm/requirements-paramrudra.lock is the exact set of package versions used for every benchmark. With newer Ray and grpcio releases, multi-node jobs fail at start-up (InvalidAuthToken, or workers timing out while they wait for the first node). The file's name says PARAM Rudra, but it is simply the tested set. Keep it.

A login node has no GPU, so the installer names CUDA 12.4 itself. At the end it prints one line with the installed versions; check that torch reports a CUDA build, not cpu:

OK  torch 2.6.0+cu124 (CUDA 12.4)  flash-attn 2.7.3  bitsandbytes 0.50.2  transformers 4.57.6  ray 2.56.1  peft 0.20.0

If the login node cannot reach the internet, the installer cannot run as it is: it needs pypi.org, download.pytorch.org and github.com. Use a machine that can, or an internal mirror; offline installs have not been tried.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the cluster profile
docs.text:
The profile tells Bhaskera what your nodes and partitions are. Copy the example and edit it:

$ cp $PREFIX/share/kit/clusters/example.yaml $PREFIX/share/kit/clusters/mycluster.yaml

name: My Cluster          # shown on the dashboard
gpus_per_node: 8
gpu_mem_gb: 80            # memory of one GPU; the "will it fit" check before a job uses it
cpus_per_node: 64         # CPUs asked for on each node
mem_per_node: 400G        # host memory asked for on each node
net_interface: ib0        # for NCCL and Ray; "" = not set
docs_url: https://example.org/bhaskera
partitions:               # smallest jobs first; max_hours is the partition's time limit
  - {max_nodes: 2,  name: debug, max_hours: 1}
  - {max_nodes: 32, name: gpu,   max_hours: 48}

Every line is optional. A job of up to max_nodes nodes goes to the first partition that fits it, with that partition's time limit. Delete param-rudra.yaml from the copy users get if you do not want it there. Check what Bhaskera reads from it:

$ BHASKERA_CLUSTER_PROFILE=$PREFIX/share/kit/clusters/mycluster.yaml \
    $PREFIX/venv/bin/python -m bhaskera.launcher.cluster_profile plan 2
debug 1 8 64 ib0 400G       # partition, hours, GPUs per node, CPUs, interface, memory: here for a job of 2 nodes

docs.title: Step 3: Make Bhaskera easy to start
docs.text:
With Lmod. Copy the modulefile and edit its first lines:

$ mkdir -p <a MODULEPATH folder>/bhaskera
$ cp slurm/modulefiles/bhaskera/1.0.0.lua <a MODULEPATH folder>/bhaskera/1.0.0.lua

Change root to your PREFIX, BHASKERA_CLUSTER_PROFILE to your profile, BHASKERA_LOGIN_HOST and BHASKERA_LOGIN_PORT to the address people use to log in over SSH (the dashboard prints the tunnel command for their laptop from them), and the manual link in help. If your cluster keeps software in a hierarchy, put the file where your other applications are.

Without modules. Users, or a small script you give them, set:

export BHASKERA_DIR=$PREFIX/src
export BHASKERA_KIT=$PREFIX/share/kit
export BHASKERA_CLUSTER_PROFILE=$PREFIX/share/kit/clusters/mycluster.yaml
export MLFLOW_ALLOW_FILE_STORE=true
export PATH=$PREFIX/venv/bin:$PATH

Then look at $PREFIX/src/bhaskera-activate.sh, which every job sources. The installer wrote it, and it loads a cuda/12.4 module when one exists. If your CUDA module has another name, edit that line. A name that cannot be loaded does not stop the job (the load is allowed to fail), so a wrong one shows only as a missing CUDA toolkit; read the first lines of a job log once.

docs.title: Step 4: Shared models and data (optional, recommended)
docs.text:
Compute nodes have no internet, so models and data must be on disk first. A shared place saves every user a download:

$ mkdir -p $(dirname $PREFIX)/models $(dirname $PREFIX)/data

The Bhaskera dashboard lists anything in models/ and data/ next to the install folder, or in the folders named by BHASKERA_MODELS and BHASKERA_DATA, under Shared on this cluster. Put Hugging Face model folders in models/ (users can also fetch their own from the Downloads menu of the page). Put tokenised data in data/ in folders named <dataset>_<model>_seq<length>_train and …_val: a tokenised folder only fits the model whose tokenizer made it. chmod -R a+rX both folders.

docs.title: Step 5: Tune what depends on your GPUs
docs.text: Setting Where Why gpu_mem_gb the cluster profile The check before a job estimates whether it fits in GPU memory. Without it, 80 GB is assumed peak_tflops_per_gpu a recipe, under monitoring: metrics: The MFU figure is measured against this peak. The default 312 is the A100's bf16 figure; use your GPU's, from the vendor's datasheet, or MFU will read wrongly net_interface the cluster profile Multi-node jobs talk over this interface. A wrong name makes NCCL slow or stuck

docs.title: Step 6: Check it as an ordinary user
docs.text:
Do this from a normal user account, not the one that installed. Each step names what should happen.

$ module load bhaskera/1.0.0                         # or the exports above
$ python -c "import torch, flash_attn, bitsandbytes, bhaskera; print('OK', torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda)"
OK 2.6.0+cu124 12.4
$ cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT ~/bhaskera-runs && cd ~/bhaskera-runs   # or any folder you choose
$ DRY_RUN=1 ./submit.sh recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml 1 1      # every check, nothing submitted

The dry run should end with RESULT: OK, or fail only on the placeholders in the sample recipe (<project>/<username>), which means the install is reading its own files. Then run something small for real:

  1. Download or copy the smallest model you have into a folder you own, and tokenise a few hundred examples (./submit.sh tokenize …, or Prepare data on the page).
  2. Make a recipe on the page (New run, Create recipe) with 10 steps, on 1 node, and Start it.
  3. In the job log you should see [step] lines with a loss, and the run should finish with training exit code: 0.
  4. Open the page from your laptop with the SSH command the module prints (bhaskera-dashboard ray --info), and check that the run, its loss curve and its GPU energy are listed.

Then try 2 nodes. A single node working does not prove the network settings: most multi-node problems show up only here.

Users need to set nothing: jobs are charged to their login name, and the page makes ~/bhaskera-runs for them on first start. If your Slurm accounts are not the login names, tell users to export SLURM_ACCOUNT=<account>. Bhaskera checks the free space of a disk before it writes anything large (checkpoints, prepared data, downloads) and refuses a job on a disk with under 1 GB free, and the page warns on Home below 20 GB; a per-user quota is not visible to it. If home folders have small quotas, tell users to keep their run folder on the large file system (cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT <big folder>/bhaskera-runs, then start the page from it): checkpoints are large.

docs.title: Where it breaks on a new cluster
docs.text: What you see Likely cause What to do No CUDA toolkit in a job, with nothing said about it The CUDA module has another name, and the failed load is ignored Edit the module line in $PREFIX/src/bhaskera-activate.sh Multi-node job hangs or is slow at the first step Wrong or missing net_interface, or a firewall between compute nodes Check ip -4 addr on two nodes; set net_interface; test with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO InvalidAuthToken, or workers waiting for the first node Ray or grpcio newer than the pinned set Reinstall with the lock file (Step 1) Job cannot be submitted: "invalid account" The Slurm account differs from the login name export SLURM_ACCOUNT=<account> Job is rejected for memory The site's default memory per node is small Set mem_per_node in the profile The site does not allow --exclusive train.sbatch asks for whole nodes Remove the --exclusive line from share/kit/train.sbatch (and its copies in users' folders) The page shows no job slots, or no limits sacctmgr is missing or accounting is off The limit checks are skipped; jobs still start "will it fit" is wrong GPUs are not 80 GB Set gpu_mem_gb in the profile Downloads, or the benchmark package, fail The login node has no internet Fetch models and data on a machine that has it, and copy them in A node is skipped for three days The node check found a fault on it (for example uncorrected GPU memory errors) It is working as intended; ask your hardware team about the node

docs.title: Keeping it up to date
docs.text:
A new version needs three things, in this order:

  1. Update the source: git -C $PREFIX/src fetch && git -C $PREFIX/src checkout <ref>.
  2. Copy the job scripts again. The install copies submit.sh, the *.sbatch files, recipes and profiles into share/kit/ as separate files, so updating the source does not update them. Rerun install-bhaskera.sh, or copy the files from $PREFIX/src/slurm/ into $PREFIX/share/kit/ yourself. Users who already copied the kit keep their own copy and have to copy the new scripts too.
  3. chmod -R a+rX $PREFIX.

Restart the dashboard after an update: a page that is already running keeps the old code.

docs.title: Parallelism Strategies
docs.text:
Strategy In plain words Use it for Avoid when DDP Every GPU holds the whole model; only the small LoRA updates cross the network Models that fit one GPU in bf16 (≈ 14 B and below) The model is larger than 80 GB QLoRA + DDP The frozen model is stored in 4-bit so it fits one GPU 70 B–123 B dense models: fastest at scale MoE models; Qwen3-235B does not fit Pipeline Model layers split into stages on different GPUs, like an assembly line Very large models and all MoE models Very small models FSDP The model is cut into pieces over all GPUs and fetched every step Only when nothing else fits Large node counts on PARAM Rudra HSDP FSDP inside small groups of GPUs As FSDP; keep a group within one node Groups spanning nodes (no gain here) DDPQLoRA + DDPPipelineFSDP / HSDP 
training:
  distributed:
    strategy: ddp

model:
  quantization: qlora
training:
  distributed:
    strategy: ddp

training:
  distributed:
    strategy: pipeline
    pipeline:
      stages: 4              # GPUs per model copy; must divide the GPU count
      microbatches: 16       # more micro-batches = less idle time
      schedule: 1f1b         # or gpipe
      activation_checkpointing: true
data:
  runtime_packing: true

training:
  distributed:
    strategy: fsdp
    fsdp:
      sharding_strategy: FULL_SHARD     # HYBRID_SHARD for HSDP
      # hsdp_shard_size: 2              # HSDP: GPUs per group (2 = one node)

Why DDP, QLoRA and Pipeline scale best on PARAM Rudra

With LoRA the base model is frozen, so DDP, QLoRA and Pipeline only send small adapter updates between nodes. FSDP and HSDP instead fetch model weights over the network every step. Without GPUDirect RDMA those transfers go through host memory, so FSDP/HSDP efficiency drops at 128 nodes (MFU 5–7%).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
A recipe is a ready Bhaskera configuration for one model, using the fastest strategy measured on PARAM Rudra.

Model QLoRA + DDP LoRA + DDP Pipeline HSDP FSDP2 Qwen/Qwen3-14B qwen3-14b-qlora qwen3-14b-ddp qwen3-14b-pipeline qwen3-14b-hsdp qwen3-14b-fsdp Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (MoE) qwen3-30b-a3b-qlora qwen3-30b-a3b-ddp qwen3-30b-a3b-pipeline qwen3-30b-a3b-hsdp qwen3-30b-a3b-fsdp meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct llama-3.3-70b-qlora — llama-3.3-70b-pipeline llama-3.3-70b-hsdp llama-3.3-70b-fsdp mistralai/Mistral-Large-Instruct-2411 mistral-large-123b-qlora — mistral-large-123b-pipeline mistral-large-123b-hsdp mistral-large-123b-fsdp Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 (MoE) — — qwen3-235b-a22b-pipeline qwen3-235b-a22b-hsdp qwen3-235b-a22b-fsdp

Each file is recipes/<name>.yaml, shown in full under Full Recipes. The fastest one for each model is in Benchmarks; in short, QLoRA + DDP for the dense 14 B to 123 B models and Pipeline for the MoE models. Node counts: any for DDP, QLoRA and FSDP2. Pipeline needs 2 GPUs per node to add up to a whole number of stages (4 stages: a multiple of 2 nodes, 8 stages: a multiple of 4, 16 stages: a multiple of 8). HSDP needs a whole number of shard groups (a group of 4 GPUs: a multiple of 2 nodes, a group of 16: a multiple of 8).

Other recipes:

Recipe Model (Hugging Face name) Strategy Node count param-1-2.9b-ddp.yaml bharatgenai/Param-1-2.9B-Instruct DDP, eager attention any param-1-7b-moe-fsdp.yaml bharatgenai/Param-1-7B FSDP any param2-17b-moe-fsdp.yaml bharatgenai/Param2-17B-A2.4B-Thinking FSDP any tokenize-chatml.yaml the model you train tokenising 1 CPU node

How the recipes relate to the benchmark

The speed and memory in each header are the measured benchmark numbers for that model and method. The recipes were written to the same settings (LoRA rank 16, sequence length 4096, the shard group sizes above) and every one loads cleanly in Bhaskera's configuration check, but a recipe is a starting point: run DRY_RUN=1 ./submit.sh recipes/<name>.yaml <nodes> 1 first, which checks the model, data, GPU memory estimate and node count without submitting.

A pipeline recipe splits the model into stages on different GPUs, so the number of GPUs (2 per node) must be a multiple of the number of stages. submit.sh checks this before it submits.

docs.title: Full Recipes
docs.text:
Every recipe in full, for reference. Open one, copy it to recipes/<name>.yaml in your run folder (they are already there when you copy the kit), replace <project>/<username> and the two tokenised data paths, and run it. The comment lines at the top give the measured speed.

Reading a recipe

  • model: the model folder, precision, attention and kernel choices, and quantization: qlora for 4-bit.
  • data: the tokenised caches (tokenized_path, val_tokenized_path), seq_len and runtime_packing.
  • lora: the adapter (r, alpha, which modules). moe: router settings for mixture-of-experts models.
  • training: batch size, learning rate, max_steps, and distributed.strategy (ddp, fsdp or pipeline, with hsdp_shard_size for HSDP and stages / microbatches for pipeline).
  • checkpoint, logging, monitoring: where checkpoints go and how often, the MLflow run name, and the metrics recorded.

# Bhaskera recipe: qwen3-14b-qlora
# Model    : Qwen/Qwen3-14B   (download to /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-14B)
# Strategy : ddp + QLoRA 4-bit
# Benchmark on PARAM Rudra (seq_len 4096, 2 x A100 80 GB per node):
#            35.5% MFU, 12.5 h/epoch on 8 nodes, 49 min on 128 nodes, 16 GB/GPU
# Nodes    : any node count
#
# Before use: replace every <project>/<username>, and set data.tokenized_path /
# data.val_tokenized_path to the two lines printed by the tokenize job.
# max_steps is 10, so a first job finishes in minutes. For a full run set it to:
#   max_steps = (training-set tokens) / (tok/s x step_s from the [step] log line)
# Run with:  ./submit.sh recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml <nodes> <hours>
model:
  name: /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-14B
  dtype: bfloat16
  attn_impl: flash_attention_2
  trust_remote_code: false
  use_liger_kernel: true
  quantization: qlora
data:
  name: local
  seq_len: 4096
  runtime_packing: true
  num_workers: 16
  tokenized_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/REPLACE_local_train_<hash>

  prefetch_batches: 2
  local_shuffle_buffer_multiplier: 10
lora:
  enabled: true
  r: 16
  alpha: 32
  dropout: 0.05
  target_modules:
  - auto
  include_experts: false
  freeze_router: true
  modules_to_save: []
training:
  batch_size: 2
  grad_accum: 1
  lr: 0.0001
  weight_decay: 0.0
  max_steps: 10
  num_epochs: 1
  warmup_steps: 50
  max_grad_norm: 1.0
  grad_clip: 1.0
  max_grad_skip_steps: 100
  seed: 42
  deterministic: false
  eval_steps: 200
  eval_batch_size: 1
  target_eval_loss: null
  distributed:
    strategy: ddp
    fsdp:
      sharding_strategy: FULL_SHARD
      transformer_layer_cls: []
      param_dtype: bfloat16
      reduce_dtype: bfloat16
      buffer_dtype: bfloat16
      activation_checkpointing: true
      cpu_offload: false
      shard_experts_individually: false
      root_reshard_after_forward: false
      forward_prefetch: true
      backward_prefetch: true
    ddp:
      find_unused_parameters: false
      gradient_as_bucket_view: true
      broadcast_buffers: false
      activation_checkpointing: true
      static_graph: false
  eval_max_rows: 1000
checkpoint:
  enabled: true
  save_dir: /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs/checkpoints/qwen3-14b-qlora
  save_interval: 1                 # epochs between checkpoints
  save_every_steps: 500            # and one every 500 steps, so a failed job loses little: continue it with ./submit.sh resume
  keep_last_n: 2
logging:
  tracker: mlflow
  project: bhaskera
  run_name: qwen3-14b-qlora
  mlflow_log_adapter: true         # keep the trained adapter with the run: Chat, Benchmark and Register need it
  mlflow_tracking_uri: ''
  log_gpu_every_n_steps: 10
monitoring:
  dashboard: true
  dashboard_host: 127.0.0.1
  dashboard_port: 8265
  metrics_export_port: 8080
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    system_every_n_steps: 1
    cuda_every_n_steps: 2
    gpu: true
    cpu: true
    cuda_memory: true
    throughput: true
    peak_tflops_per_gpu: 312.0

    throughput_warmup: 5

docs.title: Multimodal models
docs.text:
The image, video and audio starters are in configs/multimodal/ of your run folder (copied from the kit with recipes/). A run folder made earlier lacks them: cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT/configs .. Tokenise first with a tokenize_* config, which prints the two cache paths to paste in, then run the training config as its first comment lines show. See Multimodal for the data and chat.

multimodal/tokenize_vision (Tokenise images and video) configs/multimodal/tokenize_vision.yaml
# Tokenise chat data with images and video for a vision-language model (Qwen3-VL). Run once before training:
#   bhaskera-tokenize --config configs/multimodal/tokenize_vision.yaml --split both
# Only token ids, the prompt text and media paths are cached; images and video are decoded again while training.
model:
  name: /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct

data:
  name: local
  modalities: [text, image, video]      # drop what your data does not have
  train_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/train.jsonl
  val_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/val.jsonl
  seq_len: 1280
  loss_on: assistant
  image_max_pixels: 1048576             # at most 1024 visual tokens per image (32x32 px each)
  video_fps: 4
  video_max_frames: 16
  cache_dir: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache
  num_workers: 4
  tokenize_batch_size: 16
  tokenize_compression: snappy
multimodal/tokenize_audio (Tokenise audio) configs/multimodal/tokenize_audio.yaml
# Tokenise chat data with audio for an audio-language model (Qwen2.5-Omni thinker). Run once before training:
#   bhaskera-tokenize --config configs/multimodal/tokenize_audio.yaml --split both
model:
  name: /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen2.5-Omni-3B

data:
  name: local
  modalities: [text, audio]
  train_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/train.jsonl
  val_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/val.jsonl
  seq_len: 768
  audio_max_seconds: 30
  loss_on: assistant
  cache_dir: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache
  num_workers: 4
  tokenize_batch_size: 16
  tokenize_compression: snappy
multimodal/ddp (Images, DDP) configs/multimodal/ddp.yaml
# Multimodal, DDP: the whole model on every GPU. LoRA on Qwen3-VL-2B with images.
# Tokenise first (configs/multimodal/tokenize_vision.yaml), put the two printed paths below, replace <project>/<username>, then:
#   ./submit.sh configs/multimodal/ddp.yaml <nodes> <hours>

model:
  name: "/scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct"
  kind: "multimodal"
  dtype: "bfloat16"
  attn_impl: "flash_attention_2"
  use_liger_kernel: false        # compute nodes have no C headers for new Triton kernels
  freeze_encoders: ["all"]
data:
  name: "local"
  modalities: ["text", "image"]
  seq_len: 1280
  image_max_pixels: 1048576
  tokenized_path: "/scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_train_<hash>"
  num_workers: 8
  image_workers: 8
  image_prefetch_batches: 4
  local_shuffle_buffer_multiplier: 10
lora:
  enabled: true
  r: 16
  alpha: 32
  dropout: 0.05
  target_modules: ["auto"]
training:
  batch_size: 4                  # per GPU
  grad_accum: 1
  lr: 1.0e-4
  weight_decay: 0.0
  max_steps: 20
  num_epochs: 100
  warmup_steps: 2
  max_grad_norm: 1.0
  grad_clip: 1.0
  max_grad_skip_steps: 100
  eval_steps: 0
  seed: 42
  startup_timeout_s: 1800
  distributed:
    strategy: "ddp"
    ddp:
      find_unused_parameters: false   # encoders frozen; fake media keep every LoRA weight used
      gradient_as_bucket_view: true
      broadcast_buffers: false
      activation_checkpointing: true
      static_graph: false
    fsdp:
      sharding_strategy: "FULL_SHARD"
      param_dtype: "bfloat16"
      reduce_dtype: "float32"
      buffer_dtype: "bfloat16"
      activation_checkpointing: true
      shard_encoder_blocks: true
      forward_prefetch: true
      backward_prefetch: true
checkpoint:
  enabled: false
logging:
  tracker: "mlflow"
  project: "bhaskera-multimodal-scaling"
  run_name: "RUN_NAME"
  mlflow_tracking_uri: ""
monitoring:
  dashboard: false
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    system_every_n_steps: 5
    cuda_every_n_steps: 5
    throughput: true
    peak_tflops_per_gpu: 312.0
    throughput_window: 5
    throughput_warmup: 3
multimodal/fsdp (Images, FSDP2) configs/multimodal/fsdp.yaml
# Multimodal, FSDP2: the model sharded across all GPUs. LoRA on Qwen3-VL-2B with images.
# Tokenise first (configs/multimodal/tokenize_vision.yaml), put the two printed paths below, replace <project>/<username>, then:
#   ./submit.sh configs/multimodal/fsdp.yaml <nodes> <hours>

model:
  name: "/scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct"

  name: /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Param-1-2.9B-Instruct

# Bhaskera recipe: tokenize-chatml

  format_options:
    messages_field: messages

  val_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/data/val.jsonl
  seq_len: 4096
  cache_dir: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache
