  tokenize_batch_size: 64
  tokenize_compression: snappy

docs.title: Full Fine-tuning (Training Every Weight)
docs.text:
Every recipe above trains a LoRA add-on: the model stays as it is and a small adapter is trained, which is what makes 14 B to 235 B models practical. To train every weight instead, set LoRA off and use a method that spreads the model over the GPUs:

lora:
  enabled: false
training:
  lr: 1.0e-5                      # much lower than the 1e-4 of LoRA
  distributed:
    strategy: fsdp                # fsdp (FSDP2), or ddp for a model that fits on one GPU; hsdp also works
checkpoint:
  enabled: true                   # the result lives in the checkpoints, so keep this on
logging:
  mlflow_log_adapter: false       # there is no adapter to keep

docs.title: Choosing Nodes and Hours
docs.text:
Checkpoints. A checkpoint holds the trained LoRA weights and the optimizer state. With QLoRA + DDP, DDP and FSDP recipes it is written when the run ends, either at max_steps or at the end of an epoch (checkpoint.save_interval counts epochs). With Pipeline recipes it is written every save_interval steps (500 in the recipes). Resubmitting a job with the same checkpoint.save_dir continues from the latest checkpoint, and the learning-rate schedule continues with it.

So a QLoRA, DDP or FSDP run that is longer than the partition's time limit has to be split by hand: set max_steps so that each job ends before the limit, and resubmit with a larger max_steps to continue.

Time for one epoch of a 1.24-billion-token dataset (scale it by your own token count):

Recipe 8 nodes 16 nodes 32 nodes 64 nodes 128 nodes Qwen3-14B QLoRA 12.5 h 6.3 h 3.2 h 1.8 h 49 min Qwen3-30B-A3B Pipeline 12.3 h 6.1 h 3.1 h 1.6 h 53 min Llama-3.3-70B QLoRA 2.2 days 26.5 h 13.3 h 6.6 h 3.3 h Llama-3.3-70B Pipeline 2.8 days 33.7 h 16.9 h 8.4 h 4.6 h Mistral-Large-123B QLoRA 4.1 days 2.1 days 24.9 h 12.4 h 6.4 h Mistral-Large-123B Pipeline 5.2 days 2.6 days 31.3 h 15.5 h 7.8 h Qwen3-235B-A22B Pipeline 2.6 days 31.0 h 17.8 h 7.8 h 4.3 h

docs.title: Starter Configs for Other Models
docs.text:
The recipes above are tested for the models in the table. For another model, copy a starter from configs/ in the Bhaskera repository, replace the <project>/<username> paths, and run it like a recipe. There is one starter per parallelism for text and for multimodal models, and a tokenizer config for each model type:

Text Multimodal DDP configs/text/ddp.yaml configs/multimodal/ddp.yaml FSDP2 configs/text/fsdp.yaml configs/multimodal/fsdp.yaml HSDP configs/text/hsdp.yaml configs/multimodal/hsdp.yaml Pipeline configs/text/pipeline.yaml not available Tokenise first configs/text/tokenize.yaml tokenize_vision.yaml (image, video), tokenize_audio.yaml

configs/config.yaml lists every option with its default. A key that does nothing, such as a typo, is reported with the closest real name when the config is loaded.

docs.title: Saving and Finding Your Models
docs.text: A trained model is an adapter: a folder of a few hundred megabytes that sits on top of the base model. The model registry gives each adapter you want to keep a name and a version, so that "the one we use" is a name and not a run id you have to remember. It is part of MLflow, which Bhaskera already writes to, so there is nothing to set up. The Bhaskera dashboard's Models section lists every version with its alias and note.

docs.title: What gets saved, and when
docs.text:
During training, set logging.mlflow_log_adapter: true in the recipe. When the run ends, the adapter is exported in the standard PEFT format and stored with the MLflow run. Without it there is nothing to register, and neither Chat nor Benchmark can use the run.

To register at the end of training, add logging.mlflow_register_model: <name> too. Most people prefer to look at the results first:

docs.title: Register after you have looked at the results
docs.text:
On the dashboard press New run and choose Register: pick the run, give it a name (or pick a name that exists to add a new version) and, if you like, an alias of your choice and a hand-off note. In the terminal:

python -m bhaskera.launcher.register add --run <run id> --name my-assistant --alias champion \
    --note "For support questions. Weak on legal text."
python -m bhaskera.launcher.register list
python -m bhaskera.launcher.register show my-assistant:1      # the hand-off note

Each version records the run it came from, its base model, the final evaluation and any benchmark results as tags, so the registry shows what each version is without opening the run. An alias is a label you choose (champion is only an example; use your own words, such as the stage it is in) that points at one version. When a better one comes along, register it with --alias champion again and the alias moves; the old version stays.

docs.title: The hand-off note
docs.text: Each version also keeps a note for whoever picks it up next: the text you wrote (what it is for, which data, what it gets wrong), followed by what Bhaskera fills in from the run: the base model, the run, the LoRA settings, steps, learning rate, batch and sequence length, the training data, the results (evaluation loss and accuracy, benchmark scores), and how to use the adapter. The adapter needs the base model at the same path, so the note says where it was. register show <name>:<version> prints it, and the dashboard shows it when you hover over the row.

docs.title: Using a registered model
docs.text:
Everywhere a run id is accepted, a registry name works too:

./submit.sh serve --run my-assistant@champion      # chat with the champion
./submit.sh eval  --run my-assistant:3 --tasks my_test --save-samples
python -m bhaskera.launcher.register resolve my-assistant@champion     # prints the run id behind it

name means the newest version, name:3 version 3, and name@alias the version the alias points at. To load an adapter in your own code:

from mlflow.tracking import MlflowClient
from peft import PeftModel
client = MlflowClient(tracking_uri="file:///home/<you>/mlflow-runs")
folder = client.download_artifacts(run_id, "adapter")        # the run id from `register resolve`
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, folder)

docs.title: A workflow that works
docs.text:
Train with mlflow_log_adapter: true, benchmark it and test it on your own questions (see Bhaskera Dashboard), correct the data where it is wrong, train again, and register the version that is better as champion. Anyone on the project then chats with, or builds on, my-assistant@champion and never needs to know which run it was.

The registry is stored in your MLflow folder (~/mlflow-runs), so on an account that several people share, everyone sees the same models.

docs.title: When a Job Stops: Resuming
docs.text: Long jobs stop: a node fails, a job runs out of its time limit, memory runs out, or a loss spike tells you to go back. What you lose depends on the checkpoints. This page is about losing as little as possible and continuing without retyping anything.

docs.title: Checkpoints: the part you set up
docs.text:
A checkpoint is the trained adapter weights, the optimizer state and the position in the learning-rate schedule. Two settings in the recipe decide what a failure costs:

checkpoint:
  save_every_steps: 500      # a checkpoint every 500 steps (the default; 0 saves only at the end of an epoch)
  keep_last_n: 2             # how many to keep; raise it if you want to be able to go further back

Choose save_every_steps by time, not by steps. With a step of 4.7 s, 200 steps is about 16 minutes of work at risk. The checkpoint of a LoRA run is under a gigabyte, so saving often is cheap. A full fine-tune checkpoint is tens of gigabytes: save less often there. A checkpoint is also written when the run ends. A checkpoint that was still being written when the job died is ignored.

docs.title: Resuming
docs.text:
From the dashboard, a run that failed, was killed, ran out of time or stopped writing has a Resume button. In the terminal:

./submit.sh resume --run <run id>                  # the same recipe, nodes and time, from the latest checkpoint
./submit.sh resume --run <run id> --step 1000      # from an earlier checkpoint
./submit.sh resume --run <run id> --nodes 8 --hours 6
python -m bhaskera.launcher.resume show --run <run id>      # what the run left behind, without submitting

The run id is in MLflow and on the dashboard. Bhaskera takes the recipe, the number of nodes and the time limit from the job that stopped, looks for checkpoints in the folder the run saved to, and submits the job again. The job loads the checkpoint, rebuilds the learning-rate schedule at that step, and skips the training data that the earlier steps already used.

Restored: the adapter weights, the optimizer state, the position in the schedule, and the position in the training data (exactly in the first epoch; in a later epoch the data restarts at the beginning of that epoch). Not restored: the random state, so dropout differs from what an uninterrupted run would have drawn. The resumed job is a new MLflow run, tagged resumed_from with the run it continues, and its curves continue the step numbers.

docs.title: Changing something before you resume
docs.text: The recipe is read again when the job starts, so edit it first to change what the next steps do: a lower learning rate after a loss spike, a smaller batch size after running out of memory, a longer time limit. The checkpoint stays what it was. If you change the number of nodes, the global batch size changes with it (batch_size × grad_accum × GPUs); adjust grad_accum to keep it.

docs.title: Going back: a loss spike
docs.text:
If the loss jumped at step 1800 and never recovered, resume from a checkpoint before it:

python -m bhaskera.launcher.resume show --run <run id>              # lists the checkpoint steps, e.g. 1000, 1500, 2000
./submit.sh resume --run <run id> --step 1500

The checkpoints after step 1500 are renamed (rolledback-0002000), not deleted, so nothing is lost and they cannot be mistaken for the newest. Raise keep_last_n beforehand if you want more than the latest two to choose from.

docs.title: When a run cannot be resumed
docs.text: The page and the command say why: the job is still running, no checkpoint was saved (the recipe had save_every_steps: 0 and the job stopped before the first epoch ended), the recipe file is gone, or Slurm no longer remembers the job (its accounting keeps jobs for a limited time). If the recipe's checkpoint.save_dir is a relative path, submit from the folder the first job was submitted from, because a relative folder means a different place from anywhere else. An absolute path avoids the problem.

docs.title: What usually goes wrong, and what to do
docs.text: What you see Likely cause What to do The log stops with a node named in the failure summary A faulty node Resume: the node is remembered and skipped The state is TIMEOUT (MLflow shows killed) The time limit was too short Resume with --hours larger Out of memory in the failure summary Batch too large for the GPU Lower batch_size in the recipe, then resume The loss jumps and stays high Learning rate too high, or bad data Resume from before the jump with a lower lr Nothing was saved save_every_steps: 0 and the job ended mid-epoch Set it, submit again

docs.title: Start Here: Your First Run
docs.text:
This page is for someone who has never fine-tuned a model, or has never run one on a cluster. It explains the few words you need, then walks through three situations step by step, all from the command line:

  1. I have no model and no dataset: you want to see it work, or you will use a public model and dataset.
  2. I bring my own model and my own data, tokenised or not.
  3. I only want to benchmark a model I already have: no training.

What was run on PARAM Rudra for this page: option B of Case 1 (tokenise and train, end to end, with the small examples shown), the tokenising of CSV, TSV and JSON data, the checks of option A, and the benchmark of Case 3. The 14 B training of option A and the "already tokenised" route in Case 2 follow the same code but were not repeated here. A web page does the same things with buttons (Bhaskera Dashboard); this page uses the terminal because it shows exactly what happens.

docs.title: The words you will meet
docs.text: Word What it means here Model A neural network that already knows a language (Qwen3, Llama, Param). It is a folder of files: settings, a tokenizer and the weights. Fine-tuning Continuing a model's training on your own examples, so that it answers the way you need. Weights The numbers that make up a model. Training changes them. LoRA / adapter A way to fine-tune by training only a small add-on (the adapter) on top of the unchanged model. It needs far less memory and disk, and is the usual choice. QLoRA does the same on a model squeezed to 4 bits. Full fine-tuning Training every weight. It can learn more and needs far more memory (Recipes). Dataset Your examples: conversations, instructions and answers. Tokenising Turning text into the numbers a model reads. You do it once per dataset and model; every training run reuses the result (a cache). Recipe One small YAML file that says what to train, on what, and how. Step / epoch A step teaches the model one batch of examples. An epoch is one pass over all your data. Checkpoint The saved state of a run, so that one that stops can continue (resume). Benchmark A set of questions with known answers, to measure a model. Slurm job How you ask the cluster for GPUs: ./submit.sh does it for you. A node is one machine (2 GPUs on PARAM Rudra). Login node The machine you log in to. It has internet (some of them). Compute nodes, where jobs run, have none, so models and data must be on disk first.

docs.title: How a run fits together
docs.text:
model  ───┐
           ├──►  tokenise  ──►  recipe  ──►  train  ──►  check  ──►  use
 data   ───┘     (once)         (a file)    (GPUs)     (benchmark)   (chat, save)

You supply a model and data. Tokenising turns the data into numbers (a few minutes, on CPUs). A recipe names the model, the tokenised data and the settings. ./submit.sh checks the recipe, asks Slurm for GPUs and starts training. When it ends you have an adapter (or checkpoints), and you can benchmark it, chat with it and save it under a name.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Log in, load Bhaskera and make your run folder: the one place where your recipes, logs and checkpoints go.

$ ssh -p 4422 <user>@paramrudra.cdacb.in
$ module load bhaskera/1.0.0
$ cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs
$ cd /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs

Everything below is run from this folder. Jobs are charged to your login name, so there is nothing to set. Use a folder on /scratch: checkpoints can be large, and home folders fill up quickly.

Already on PARAM Rudra: models and data are waiting

The administrators keep ready-to-use models in /home/apps/bhaskera/models (Qwen3-14B, Param-1-2.9B-Instruct, Param-1-7B, Param2-17B, and the multimodal Qwen3-VL and Qwen2.5-Omni) and tokenised data in /home/apps/bhaskera/data (nemotron-chat_<model>_seq4096_train and _val for three of the models, with a README.txt). You can point a recipe straight at them.

docs.title: Case 1: I have no model and no dataset
docs.text: Two ways. Option A needs no download at all; option B shows how to use any public model and dataset by name.

docs.title: Option A: use what is already on the cluster
docs.text:
Copy a ready recipe, then change the lines below in your copy (open it with any editor, for example nano):

$ cp recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml recipes/my-first-run.yaml

model:
  name: /home/apps/bhaskera/models/Qwen3-14B                                       # the shared model
data:
  tokenized_path: /home/apps/bhaskera/data/nemotron-chat_qwen3-14b_seq4096_train   # the shared, already tokenised data
  val_tokenized_path: /home/apps/bhaskera/data/nemotron-chat_qwen3-14b_seq4096_val
checkpoint:
  save_dir: /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs/checkpoints/my-first-run   # your own folder
logging:
  run_name: my-first-run                                                           # how the run is named in MLflow

Check it first. This runs every check and submits nothing:

$ DRY_RUN=1 ./submit.sh recipes/my-first-run.yaml 1 1
== preflight (login node, a few seconds) ==
[PASS] model weights              8 safetensors file(s) in /home/apps/bhaskera/models/Qwen3-14B
[PASS] tokenizer                  Qwen2TokenizerFast, vocab 151669
...
[PASS] est. per-GPU @ 2 GPUs      17.6 GiB of 80.0 GiB
RESULT: OK
dry run: every check passed; nothing was submitted

Then run it. The arguments are the recipe, the number of nodes and the hours. The recipe trains for only 10 steps, so a first run is over in minutes:

$ ./submit.sh recipes/my-first-run.yaml 1 1
submitted job <id>: my-first-run on 1 nodes (2 GPUs), gpu-debug, 1 h
$ tail -f logs/my-first-run_<id>.out | grep --line-buffered -E '\[step|eval|exit code'

You will see one line per step with the loss (how wrong the model still is: it should fall), and the run ends with === training exit code: 0 ===. See Monitoring for what each number means.

docs.title: Option B: a public model and dataset, by name
docs.text:
Here the model and the dataset live on Hugging Face. You do not download them yourself: name them, and Bhaskera fetches them first. This example uses a small model (Qwen3-0.6B) and the public Alpaca instruction dataset, so it is quick.

1. Tokenise. Save this as recipes/alpaca-tokenize.yaml:

model:
  name: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B                     # a Hugging Face model, by name
data:
  name: local
  format: alpaca                            # the dataset has instruction / input / output columns
  train_path: hf://tatsu-lab/alpaca         # a Hugging Face dataset, by name
  seq_len: 512                              # longest example, in tokens
  cache_dir: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache
  num_workers: 8
  tokenize_batch_size: 64

$ ./submit.sh tokenize recipes/alpaca-tokenize.yaml
downloading model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B (main): 1.4 GB in 10 files -> .../models/Qwen__Qwen3-0.6B
downloading dataset tatsu-lab/alpaca (main): 0.0 GB in 3 files -> .../data/hf/tatsu-lab__alpaca
resolved: model.name -> .../models/Qwen__Qwen3-0.6B; data.train_path -> .../_splits/train
Submitted batch job <id>

What happened: ./submit.sh saw two Hugging Face names, downloaded them into models/ and data/hf/ in your run folder (on a login node that has internet; some do not, and this is handled for you, see the note below), and ran a resolved copy of your recipe with the real folders in it. Your recipe is unchanged, and a download that finished is not repeated.

The tokenise job takes a few minutes on CPUs (52,000 examples). When it ends, its log prints the cache path:

$ grep -a "tokenized_path" logs/bhaskera-tokenize_<id>.out
║   tokenized_path: ".../cache/local_train_<hash>"

Alpaca has a training part only, so this tokenises training data (52,002 examples) and says that no validation file was set.

2. Make the training recipe from a ready one: copy it, then change these lines in your copy:

$ cp recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml recipes/alpaca-small.yaml

model:
  name: Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B                       # the Hugging Face name again; it was downloaded in step 1
data:
  seq_len: 512
  tokenized_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_train_<hash>    # the path printed above
  # delete the val_tokenized_path line: Alpaca has no validation part
training:
  eval_steps: 0                               # no validation data, so no evaluation
checkpoint:
  save_dir: /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs/checkpoints/alpaca-small
logging:
  run_name: alpaca-small

3. Check, then run:

$ DRY_RUN=1 ./submit.sh recipes/alpaca-small.yaml 1 1        # every check; nothing submitted
$ ./submit.sh recipes/alpaca-small.yaml 1 1
submitted job <id>: alpaca-small on 1 nodes (2 GPUs), gpu-debug, 1 h

The log shows lines like [epoch 0][step 8] loss=2.54 ..., and ends with === training exit code: 0 ===. In this example the ten steps took about seven seconds of training (a 0.6 B model on 2 GPUs); loading the model takes most of the time.

No internet on the login node you landed on?

On PARAM Rudra only some login nodes (login01, login02, login03, login05) can reach the internet. If you are on another one, downloads run on one that can, over SSH, and say so (downloading on login01 ...). If it cannot find one, it tells you what to do. See Downloads and Dataset Versions.

You can also download by hand: python -m bhaskera.downloads get --kind model --repo Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --target <folder> (--kind dataset for data), and look before downloading with python -m bhaskera.downloads preview ....

docs.title: Case 2: I bring my own model and my own data
Your model
docs.text:
A model is a Hugging Face model folder: it has a config.json, the weight files (.safetensors), and the tokenizer files, all in one folder. Put it on /scratch, for example /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/MyModel, and name that folder in the recipe: model.name: /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/MyModel.

  • A model that comes with its own Python code (the BharatGen Param models, for example) needs trust_remote_code: true.
  • Compute nodes have no internet, so the whole folder must be there, tokenizer included.
  • Which models work: the ones listed under Recipes have been tried. Others may work if they use a standard architecture; the check before a run (DRY_RUN=1) tells you if the files, the tokenizer and the memory fit are right.

docs.title: Your data, not tokenised yet
docs.text:
Raw data can be a file, a folder or a pattern, in JSONL, JSON, CSV, TSV, Parquet, Arrow or plain text (optionally .gz): see what formats work. What matters is the columns, set with data.format:

data.format Each row needs Example chatml messages: a list of {role, content} {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}]} alpaca instruction, output, optionally input {"instruction": "...", "input": "", "output": "..."} sharegpt conversations: a list of {from, value} {"conversations": [{"from": "human", "value": "..."}, {"from": "gpt", "value": "..."}]} prompt_completion prompt and completion (other column names: format_options: {prompt_field: question, completion_field: answer}) {"prompt": "...", "completion": "..."}

Put a few hundred examples aside as a validation file; the run uses it to show whether the model is really improving. Then copy the tokenise recipe, fill in your paths, and run it:

$ cp recipes/tokenize-chatml.yaml recipes/my-tokenize.yaml
$ nano recipes/my-tokenize.yaml          # model.name, data.format, train_path, val_path, seq_len, cache_dir
$ ./submit.sh tokenize recipes/my-tokenize.yaml

Before tokenising, python -m bhaskera.launcher.data_tools inspect <file.jsonl> --format chatml --seq-len 4096 finds empty answers, duplicates and rows that are too long (these helper tools read JSONL; other formats are read directly by the tokenise step). If you have a validation file (val_path), you get a second cache; if not, only the training data is tokenised and the log says so.

Tokenised data fits one model

The numbers depend on the model's tokenizer and on seq_len. A cache made for Qwen3-14B is right for Qwen3 models, not for Llama. Tokenise again for another family.

docs.title: Your data, already tokenised
docs.text:
If your data is already tokenised, skip the step above. Bhaskera trains from a folder of Parquet files with these columns:

Column What input_ids the token numbers labels the same length: the numbers to learn (use -100 for a position that should not count) attention_mask 1 for a real token, 0 for padding. If you have none, set data.pack_sequences: true and an all-ones mask is made.

If your columns have other names, rename them in the recipe with data.column_map: {your_name: input_ids}. Point the recipe at the folder:

data:
  name: local
  seq_len: 4096                       # the length of your rows: it must match, rows are never re-padded
  tokenized_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/mydata/train_tokenised
  val_tokenized_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/mydata/val_tokenised     # optional

Write a small metadata.json next to the Parquet files if you can ({"model_name": "<model folder>", "seq_len": 4096}): without it Bhaskera cannot check the length and tokenizer against your model, and warns instead. Data you tokenised yourself works from the command line; the web page lists only caches that have a metadata.json.

docs.title: Train
docs.text:
Copy a ready recipe for your model size (see Recipes), and set the model, the data and the folder for checkpoints:

$ cp recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml recipes/my-run.yaml
$ nano recipes/my-run.yaml        # model.name, tokenized_path, val_tokenized_path, checkpoint.save_dir, logging.run_name, max_steps
$ DRY_RUN=1 ./submit.sh recipes/my-run.yaml 8 12       # every check, nothing submitted: recipe, nodes, hours
$ ./submit.sh recipes/my-run.yaml 8 12

max_steps is 10 in the ready recipes so that a first job finishes in minutes. For a real run set it from your data size (the comment at the top of each recipe says how). DRY_RUN checks the files, the tokenizer, whether the model fits in GPU memory, the partition limits, the disk space for checkpoints and whether your data changed since it was registered.

To train every weight instead of a LoRA add-on, see Full fine-tuning.

If a job stops half way: ./submit.sh resume --run <run id> continues from the last checkpoint (Resuming a Job).

docs.title: Case 3: Benchmark a model you already have
docs.text:
You do not need to train anything to measure a model. You need the model folder and the benchmark data.

1. Prepare the benchmark data once. It is downloaded into your run folder. Compute nodes have no internet, so do this on a login node that has it (login01, login02, login03 or login05 on PARAM Rudra):

$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate prepare --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag,winogrande
downloading arc_easy ...
done: the datasets are in the Hugging Face cache

2. Run the benchmark on a GPU node:

$ ./submit.sh eval --model /home/apps/bhaskera/models/Qwen3-14B --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag --limit 200 --out qwen3-14b.json
submitted job <id>: evaluation, gpu-debug, 1 h
$ tail -f logs/bhaskera-eval_<id>.out

--limit 200 uses 200 questions per test for a quick look; leave it out for the full test. --model is any model folder (yours, a shared one, or one you downloaded). With no adapter given, only that base model is measured. In a check we ran this way on Qwen3-0.6B with 50 questions of arc_easy:

no adapter given: only the base model is evaluated
arc_easy: acc_norm = 0.6000
saved .../case3_arc.json
=== evaluation exit code: 0 ===

3. Compare models. Run it again for another model with another --out, then read both:

$ ./submit.sh eval --model /home/apps/bhaskera/models/Param-1-7B --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag --limit 200 --out param-1-7b.json
$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate show qwen3-14b.json
$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate show param-1-7b.json

4. Test on your own questions. The standard tests say little about your own use. Put question and answer pairs in a JSONL file ({"question": "...", "answer": "..."} per line), turn it into a test, and run it the same way:

$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate init-task --name my_test --data /scratch/<project>/<username>/my.jsonl
$ ./submit.sh eval --model <model folder> --tasks my_test --save-samples
$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate review <samples folder>      # what is right, what is wrong, with the answers

The result is saved in the --out file. Add --mlflow to keep it in MLflow too. Once you have trained a model, --run <run id> (or a registered name) benchmarks it against its base model in one go (Bhaskera Dashboard and Model Registry).

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text: What you see What to do RESULT: FAIL in the dry run Read the [FAIL] line: it names the file, library or setting. Fix it, run the dry run again. The job stays queued The partition is busy or you hit its limit. squeue -u $USER shows it, and ./submit.sh told you the limits before submitting. not enough space for ... A disk is full or nearly full. Choose a folder on a bigger disk, keep fewer checkpoints. "cannot reach the internet" on a download You are on a login node without internet and none was found to use. See Troubleshooting. The run stopped half way ./submit.sh resume --run <run id>. Anything else Troubleshooting lists the common errors, and a failed job ends with a plain explanation.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Recipes: ready recipes for each model, and how many nodes and hours to ask for.
  • Data Format: file types, column layouts and plain text.
  • Downloads and Dataset Versions: downloading, and naming and versioning your data.
  • Monitoring: reading the step log, MLflow, and the GPU energy a run used.
  • Bhaskera Dashboard: the same things with buttons, plus chat with the model you trained.
  • Model Registry: keep a trained model under a name, with a note.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom (in the job log) Cause What to do InvalidAuthToken: Authentication token is missing or incorrect, job ends after ~15 s Ray newer than 2.56 in your own installation Install the pinned versions from Installation Timed out while waiting for GCS to become available Ray could not start on the job's first node Resubmit; if it repeats on the same node, exclude it (below) torch.version.cuda is None, or CUDA built: None after setup.sh setup.sh ran on a login node without BHASKERA_CUDA=12.4 Delete .venv and rerun BHASKERA_CUDA=12.4 bash setup.sh preflight reported FAIL from submit.sh The run does not fit in GPU memory as configured Use the QLoRA or Pipeline recipe, more stages, or batch_size: 1 CUDA out of memory Model or batch too large for the strategy As above; lower batch_size and raise grad_accum node running low on memory (Ray kills workers) Host RAM (about 187 GB per node) exhausted while loading a very large model Use the Pipeline recipe for that model invalid device ordinal A GPU on one node failed to start Resubmit with that node excluded DistBackendError or an NCCL timeout Network fault or a hung process Resubmit; if it repeats on one node, exclude it oom_kill events in a tokenize job The tokenize job ran with a small default memory Use the provided tokenize.sbatch (--exclusive --mem=180G)

docs.title: Excluding a faulty node
docs.text:
Find the node behind a failing worker from the address in the log (ip=172.41.x.y):

$ grep -w 172.41.x.y /etc/hosts
172.41.x.y cbgpuXXXX-ib0 cbgpuXXXX-ib0.cdacb.in

Then keep your jobs off it. submit.sh passes BHASKERA_EXCLUDE to sbatch --exclude:

$ export BHASKERA_EXCLUDE=cbgpuXXXX          # comma-separated for several nodes
$ ./submit.sh recipes/<recipe>.yaml 8 12

Note

The SBATCH_EXCLUDE environment variable is not applied on PARAM Rudra; use BHASKERA_EXCLUDE (or --exclude= when calling sbatch yourself).

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• QLoRA, DDP and FSDP recipes write a checkpoint only when the run ends, so a run longer than the time limit has to be split with max_steps (see Choosing Nodes and Hours). Pipeline recipes checkpoint every 500 steps. All of them continue from the latest checkpoint when resubmitted, but the data starts again from the beginning of the training set.
  • MoE models are slow outside the Pipeline strategy (0.2–1.7% MFU), because the standard expert code processes experts one at a time. Use the Pipeline recipes for MoE models. -

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text: Task Command Load Bhaskera module load bhaskera/1.0.0 (own installation: source $BHASKERA_DIR/.venv/bin/activate) Get the job scripts and recipes cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs Download a model (login node) huggingface-cli download <org>/<model> --local-dir /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/<model> Tokenise ./submit.sh tokenize recipes/tokenize-chatml.yaml Train (recipe, nodes, hours) ./submit.sh recipes/<recipe>.yaml 8 12 Follow the log tail -f logs/<recipe>_<jobid>.out \| grep -E '\[step\|eval\|exit code' Check a recipe without submitting python -m bhaskera.launcher.preflight --config recipes/<recipe>.yaml --num-gpus 16 MLflow dashboard bhaskera-dashboard start --port 5055 / status / tunnel / stop Bhaskera Dashboard: jobs, start, chat bhaskera-dashboard ray (see Bhaskera Dashboard) Chat with a trained run ./submit.sh serve --run <run id> Benchmark a trained run ./submit.sh eval --run <run id> --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag --limit 200 Continue a run that stopped ./submit.sh resume --run <run id> (add --step N to go back) Save a trained model in the registry python -m bhaskera.launcher.register add --run <run id> --name <model> --alias champion (see Model Registry) Hyperparameter sweep python -m bhaskera.launcher.sweep plan\|submit\|report sweep.yaml Check and clean a data file python -m bhaskera.launcher.data_tools inspect\|dedupe\|filter\|split

docs.title: The MLflow link says the site cannot be reached
docs.text:
The page's links to MLflow and to each job's Ray Dashboard use addresses like mlflow.localhost:8265, which go through the same SSH tunnel as the page itself.

  • If the page opens but mlflow.localhost is refused, the browser may be trying the IPv6 address (::1) while your tunnel listens on IPv4 only. Add a second forward to the SSH command, -L [::1]:8265:localhost:<port>, or use Chrome or Firefox, which resolve *.localhost themselves.
  • If MLflow itself is not running on the login node, start it with bhaskera-dashboard start.
  • The Bhaskera dashboard's Models and Runs sections do not need MLflow's page: they read the same files directly. On PARAM Rudra the module is found on every login node except login04, whose MODULEPATH lacks /home/apps/AIStack (a setup difference on that node, not a Bhaskera fault). Use another login node, or add the path yourself: module use /home/apps/AIStack, then load it. If it is unknown elsewhere, the module cache may be out of date: module --ignore_cache load bhaskera/1.0.0.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Fine-tuning a large language model on many GPU nodes usually means writing your own launch scripts, choosing a parallelism strategy by trial and error, and finding out about memory limits after the job has waited in the queue. Bhaskera packages all of that for PARAM Rudra: you pick a recipe, give it your data and a node count, and it runs. Every recipe in this guide has been run on PARAM Rudra, and the numbers below come from those runs.

docs.title: What You Get
docs.text:
• Speed that scales with the number of nodes. QLoRA recipes keep 34–39% MFU from 8 to 128 nodes, and Pipeline recipes 23–31% on dense models. Going from 8 to 128 nodes makes Qwen3-14B about 15 times faster (12.5 h to 49 min per epoch).
  • Large models on 80 GB GPUs. QLoRA stores the frozen model in 4 bits: Llama-3.3-70B needs 55 GB per GPU instead of 141 GB, and Mistral-Large-123B fits as well. Pipeline trains Qwen3-235B at 45 GB per GPU.
  • A check before the job is queued. submit.sh runs a preflight on the login node in seconds. It checks the model files, libraries and data, and estimates GPU memory to about 15% of the measured peak, so a job that cannot fit is rejected before it waits in the queue.
  • One file per run. A recipe holds the model, the data and the strategy. Recipes for eight model and strategy combinations are included; change two paths and submit.

docs.title: What each optimisation saves
docs.text:
Each optimisation was switched off on its own for the same run: Qwen3-14B, QLoRA, 5 nodes (10 GPUs), sequence length 4096, 10 steps. Only one setting differs between rows.

Run Step time MFU Peak GPU memory Real tokens / s Compared with the full setup All on (recipe as shipped) 4.78 s 35.4% 16.0 GB 17,156 Triton kernels (Liger) off 5.27 s 32.1% 29.9 GB 15,551 10% slower, +13.9 GB (1.9× the memory) Sequence packing off 4.73 s 35.8%* 16.0 GB 9,826 1.75× slower (42.5% of every batch is padding) Flash-attention off (PyTorch attention, no packing) 5.96 s 28.4% 16.2 GB 8,176 2.1× slower in total

* MFU counts padding as work, so it does not drop when packing is switched off; the real tokens per second do.

docs.title: What that means for a full epoch
docs.text:
For a 1.24-billion-token dataset, scaling the measured Qwen3-14B QLoRA times (12.5 h on 8 nodes, 49 min on 128 nodes) by the ratios above:

Setup 8 nodes 128 nodes All on 12.5 h 49 min Triton kernels off 13.8 h (+1.3 h) 54 min Packing off 21.8 h (+9.3 h) 1 h 26 min Flash-attention and packing off 26.2 h (+13.7 h) 1 h 43 min

docs.title: What each one does
docs.text: Optimisation What it does What it saves Triton kernels (Liger) Normalisation, rotary embedding, SwiGLU and the loss run as fused GPU kernels written in Triton. The loss is computed in chunks, so the full table of scores over the whole vocabulary (151,936 words for each of the 8,192 tokens one GPU handles per step) is never stored. 46% less GPU memory (29.9 → 16.0 GB) and 10% faster steps. The memory saving is what leaves room for a larger batch or a longer sequence. Sequence packing Short conversations are joined into full 4096-token rows. 1.75× more real tokens per second: on this dataset 42.5% of an unpacked batch is padding. Flash-attention 2 Computes attention in small tiles in fast on-chip memory (a CUDA kernel, not Triton). 1.26× faster steps (5.96 s vs 4.73 s, both without packing). It is also what makes packing possible. Memory is about the same here, because PyTorch's own attention already avoids the large attention table. QLoRA Stores the frozen model in 4 bits. Qwen3-14B: 32 → 16 GB per GPU and 31.6% → 35.5% MFU (8 nodes). Llama-3.3-70B: the bf16 weights alone are 141 GB and cannot fit on an 80 GB GPU; with QLoRA the measured peak is 55 GB.

docs.title: Other measured effects
docs.text:
What Bhaskera does Effect, measured Why Choosing the right strategy Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE), 128 nodes: 33.4 h with FSDP → 53 min with Pipeline (38× faster) FSDP moves model weights between nodes every step; Pipeline and QLoRA move only small adapter updates Fast MoE experts (Pipeline) Qwen3-30B-A3B: 71.3 → 37.3 s per step (1.9×); Qwen3-235B: 88.3 → 47.0 s (1.9×) Frozen experts are computed as a few large matrix multiplications instead of one small one per expert Linear scaling Qwen3-14B QLoRA: 27,463 → 424,899 tokens/s from 8 to 128 nodes (15.5× for 16× the nodes) With LoRA, nodes exchange only adapter gradients

How these were measured

The four runs above are single 10-step runs on the same dataset, so treat differences of a few percent as noise. The size of each effect depends on the model: the Triton-kernel memory saving, for example, grows with the vocabulary size and the batch.

docs.title: How It Is Built
docs.text:
Bhaskera is a Python package built on PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and PEFT, with Ray for starting and coordinating the processes across nodes.

Layer What it does Job scripts submit.sh checks the recipe and picks the partition; train.sbatch starts one Ray cluster across the job's nodes over InfiniBand Data Text is tokenised once into a Parquet cache; each GPU reads its own share, and sequences are packed on the fly Model Any Hugging Face causal language model; Bhaskera inspects it to find its layers, experts, routers and LoRA targets, so no model-specific code is needed Parallelism QLoRA + DDP, DDP, Pipeline (1F1B / GPipe), FSDP2 and HSDP, chosen with one line in the recipe Training loop LoRA training with evaluation (loss and next-token accuracy), MoE load-balancing losses, checkpoints, and one metrics line per step

docs.title: Who It Is For
docs.text:
• Researchers and students who want to adapt an open model (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, BharatGen Param) to their own data without writing distributed-training code.
  • Teams with large models: 70 B–235 B models on 8–128 nodes, with tables showing how long each takes before you submit.
  • Anyone new to PARAM Rudra: the job scripts handle Ray, NCCL, InfiniBand and partition limits.

Start with Installation and the End-to-end Example.

docs.title: End-to-end Example
docs.text:
New to this?

Start Here: Your First Run explains the words and walks through three cases (no model and no data, your own model and data, benchmarking a model you have). This page is the longer example with the 14 B model.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This page takes one model, Qwen3-14B, from raw data to a trained LoRA adapter, using the qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml recipe. Every other recipe works the same way; only the model and the node count change (see Recipes).

The run has nine steps, all started from a login node. Steps 1 to 4 train the model; steps 5 to 9 are what you do with it afterwards.

  1. Download the model and prepare the data
  2. Tokenise the data (one CPU job, once per model and dataset)
  3. Run a short first job (10 steps)
  4. Run the full training job
  5. Watch it: MLflow, and optionally the Ray Dashboard and Grafana
  6. Chat with the trained model (serve)
  7. Evaluate it on your own questions
  8. Benchmark it against the base model
  9. Save it under a name (register)

docs.title: Run folder
docs.text:
$ module load bhaskera/1.0.0
$ cp -r $BHASKERA_KIT /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs
$ cd /scratch/<project>/<username>/bhaskera-runs

Jobs are charged to your login name, which is your Slurm account on PARAM Rudra, so there is nothing to set. If you work under another account, export SLURM_ACCOUNT=<account> first. The run folder holds recipes, logs and checkpoints (large for big models), so a folder on /scratch is the usual choice. If you make none, the dashboard creates ~/bhaskera-runs from the shared kit the first time it starts.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Compute nodes have no internet access, so download the model on a login node:

$ huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen3-14B --local-dir /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-14B

Note

Llama and Mistral models are gated: accept the licence on the model's Hugging Face page, then run huggingface-cli login --token <your_token> once before downloading.

docs.title: Training data
docs.text:
One conversation per line in a JSONL file, in ChatML form:

{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is HPC?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "High-performance computing is ..."}]}

Put a separate validation file next to it (a few hundred to a few thousand conversations):

/scratch/<project>/<username>/data/train.jsonl
/scratch/<project>/<username>/data/val.jsonl

alpaca (instruction, input, output), sharegpt (conversations with from / value) and prompt_completion (prompt, completion) files also work: set data.format in the tokenize recipe.

docs.title: Step 1: Tokenise
docs.text:
Tokenising turns text into the numbers the model reads. It is done once; every training run reuses the result. In recipes/tokenize-chatml.yaml, replace <project>/<username> and set model.name to the model you will train, then submit:

$ ./submit.sh tokenize recipes/tokenize-chatml.yaml

docs.title: Sample SLURM script
docs.text:
submit.sh runs tokenize.sbatch on one CPU node of the debug partition:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=bhaskera-tokenize
#SBATCH --partition=debug
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=48
#SBATCH --exclusive
#SBATCH --mem=180G                     # debug partition maximum per node
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out

set -uo pipefail
CONFIG="${1:?usage: sbatch tokenize.sbatch <tokenize-config.yaml>}"
: "${BHASKERA_DIR:?export BHASKERA_DIR=/scratch/<project>/<username>/Bhaskera before submitting}"
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 HF_DATASETS_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1
source "$BHASKERA_DIR/bhaskera-activate.sh"
export RAY_TMPDIR="/tmp/ray_${SLURM_JOB_ID}"

python -m bhaskera.launcher.tokenize --config "$CONFIG" --split both
echo "=== tokenize exit code: $? ==="

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
The end of logs/bhaskera-tokenize_<jobid>.out (3,000 conversations took under 4 minutes):

║   [train] /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_train_d9cc22aaa7a4fdb4
║   [val] /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_val_eb6d6d3703815f3c
║
║ Paste this into your training config:
║
║ data:
║   name: "local"
║   seq_len: 4096
║   format: "chatml"
║   tokenized_path: "/scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_train_d9cc22aaa7a4fdb4"
║   val_tokenized_path: "/scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_val_eb6d6d3703815f3c"
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

=== tokenize exit code: 0 ===

docs.title: Step 2: Edit the Recipe
docs.text:
Open recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml, replace <project>/<username>, and paste the two paths:

model:
  name: /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-14B
data:
  tokenized_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_train_d9cc22aaa7a4fdb4
  val_tokenized_path: /scratch/<project>/<username>/cache/local_val_eb6d6d3703815f3c

docs.title: Step 3: First Run (10 steps)
docs.text:
The recipe runs 10 steps. Submit it on 8 nodes with a 1-hour limit:

$ ./submit.sh recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml 8 1

submit.sh first checks the recipe on the login node (model files, libraries, data, and whether it fits in GPU memory), then picks the partition and submits:

== preflight (login node, a few seconds) ==
Preflight: recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml
[PASS] model weights              8 safetensors file(s) in /scratch/<project>/<username>/models/Qwen3-14B
[PASS] tokenizer                  Qwen2TokenizerFast, vocab 151669
[PASS] flash-attn                 2.7.3 imports against this torch
[PASS] liger-kernel               imports
[PASS] tokenized_path             1 parquet file(s), seq_len/model match
[PASS] val_tokenized_path         1 parquet file(s), seq_len/model match
[INFO] weights                    9.9 GB in 4-bit NF4 (QLoRA) (40 layers, ~0.17 GB per layer unit)
[PASS] est. per-GPU @ 16 GPUs     17.6 GiB of 80.0 GiB
[PASS] min GPUs (DDP)             any count (full replica fits)
RESULT: OK
submitted job <jobid>: qwen3-14b-qlora on 8 nodes (16 GPUs), gpu-small, 1 h
follow it:  tail -f logs/qwen3-14b-qlora_<jobid>.out | grep --line-buffered -E '\[step|eval|exit code'

docs.title: Sample SLURM script
docs.text:
train.sbatch starts a Ray cluster across all nodes of the job over InfiniBand and one training worker per GPU:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=bhaskera
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=48
#SBATCH --exclusive
#SBATCH --mem=170G                     # host RAM per node; the GPU partitions default to only 20 GB
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out

set -uo pipefail
CONFIG="${1:?usage: sbatch train.sbatch <config.yaml>}"
: "${BHASKERA_DIR:?export BHASKERA_DIR=/scratch/<project>/<username>/Bhaskera before submitting}"

export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 HF_DATASETS_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1
export MLFLOW_ALLOW_FILE_STORE=true
source "$BHASKERA_DIR/bhaskera-activate.sh"

export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=ib0 NCCL_DEBUG=WARN NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1
export NCCL_TIMEOUT=3600 TORCH_NCCL_BLOCKING_WAIT=1 TORCH_DISTRIBUTED_TIMEOUT=3600
export PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True
if grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*strategy:[[:space:]]*"?ddp' "$CONFIG"; then CDMC=1; else CDMC=32; fi
export CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=${CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS:-$CDMC}

nodes=($(scontrol show hostnames "$SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"))
head_ip=$(srun --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 -w "${nodes[0]}" ip -4 addr show ib0 | awk '/inet / {print $2}' | cut -d/ -f1)
if [[ -z "$head_ip" ]]; then
    echo "=== could not read the ib0 address of ${nodes[0]} (Slurm controller unreachable or ib0 down); resubmit ==="
    exit 1
fi
port=$(( 6379 + SLURM_JOB_ID % 1000 ))
export RAY_ADDRESS="${head_ip}:${port}" RAY_TMPDIR="/tmp/ray_${SLURM_JOB_ID}" RAY_raylet_start_wait_time_s=300
GPUS_PER_NODE=2
WORKERS=$(( SLURM_NNODES * GPUS_PER_NODE ))

srun --nodes="$SLURM_NNODES" --ntasks="$SLURM_NNODES" \
    ray symmetric-run --address "$RAY_ADDRESS" --min-nodes "$SLURM_NNODES" \
        --num-cpus="$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" --num-gpus="$GPUS_PER_NODE" \
        -- \
        python -m bhaskera.launcher.train --config "$CONFIG" --num-workers "$WORKERS" --no-dashboard
RC=$?
echo "=== training exit code: $RC ==="
exit $RC

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text:
The first step appears after Ray start-up and model loading (about 5 minutes for a 14 B model, 10–20 minutes for 70 B–235 B). The last lines of a Qwen3-14B QLoRA run on 8 nodes:

[epoch 0][step 9] loss=1.1703 lr=1.81e-05 grad_norm=0.2473 tok/s=27711 MFU=35.8% HFU=53.2% pad=0% step_s=4.70 MFU_step=36.0% mem=16.0/16.3GiB
[epoch 0][step 10] loss=1.0350 lr=2.01e-05 grad_norm=0.2650 tok/s=27620 MFU=35.7% HFU=53.0% pad=0% step_s=4.81 MFU_step=35.2% mem=16.0/16.3GiB
[epoch 0][step 10] eval_loss=1.5705 eval_acc=0.6557
=== training exit code: 0 ===

What each field means is explained in Monitoring.

docs.title: Step 4: Full Run
docs.text:
Work out the number of steps for one pass over your data from the first run:

max_steps = (tokens in your training set) / (tok/s × step_s)

For example, with 1.24 billion tokens and the run above: 1,240,000,000 / (27,620 × 4.81) ≈ 9,300 steps. Set max_steps in the recipe, check Choosing Nodes and Hours, and submit:

$ ./submit.sh recipes/qwen3-14b-qlora.yaml 8 20

A checkpoint with the trained LoRA weights and the optimizer state is written to checkpoint.save_dir when the run ends. Submitting the job again with the same save_dir and a larger max_steps continues from it.

Keep the adapter

Steps 6 to 9 use the adapter the run stores, which needs logging.mlflow_log_adapter: true. The shipped recipes and the recipes the dashboard writes set it. A full fine-tune stores no adapter, so it has no Chat, Benchmark by run or Register.

Steps 5 to 9 need the run id of the finished training run: the 32-character id in the Runs table of the dashboard (and in MLflow's run page). Every command below can also be done with a button on the Bhaskera dashboard; the commands are shown because they work from any terminal.

docs.title: Step 5: Watch It (MLflow, Ray Dashboard, Grafana)
docs.text:
Open the dashboard on a login node. Run this on your laptop and leave it open (the command comes from bhaskera-dashboard ray --info; add --node login01 to land on a login node of your choice, and see Monitoring):

$ ssh -p 4422 -L 8265:localhost:<port> <user>@paramrudra.cdacb.in "bash -lc 'module load bhaskera/1.0.0 && bhaskera-dashboard ray'"

Then open http://localhost:8265.

Tool Use it for Needs MLflow The run's loss and evaluation curves, throughput, GPU energy and the model registry, kept after the job ends Nothing extra (the dashboard starts it) Ray Dashboard (optional) While the job runs: every node's CPU, memory and GPU load, the workers and their logs. Open it on the job's card A running job Grafana (optional), shown as GPU charts GPU, CPU and memory over time for every node Prometheus and Grafana installed next to Bhaskera; without them the other two still work

To look at MLflow alone, without the dashboard, run bhaskera-dashboard start on a login node and bhaskera-dashboard tunnel prints the command for your laptop. MLflow started this way stops when the login session that started it ends.

docs.title: Step 6: Chat With the Trained Model
docs.text:
$ ./submit.sh serve --run <run id>                 # prints the job number
$ tail -f logs/bhaskera-serve_<job>.out            # wait for: === serving on <node>:<port> ===

Loading takes 5 to 8 minutes for a 14 B model. On the dashboard, press Chat on the run instead: the window opens by itself when the model is ready, with Tuned, Base and Compare answers side by side. From a terminal, link to the node from the login node and ask:

$ ssh -N -L <port>:localhost:<port> <node> &
$ curl -s localhost:<port>/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
       -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is HPC?"}], "max_tokens": 200}'

Add "use_adapter": false to get the base model's answer from the same weights. The server stops after two hours (SERVE_HOURS changes it) or with scancel <job>, which frees the GPU node.

docs.title: Step 7: Evaluate on Your Own Questions
docs.text:
Standard benchmarks say little about your own use, so test the model on examples from your work. Put them in a JSONL file, one {"question": "...", "answer": "..."} per line, then:

$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate init-task --name my_test --data /scratch/<project>/<username>/my.jsonl
$ ./submit.sh eval --run <run id> --tasks my_test --save-samples
$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate review <folder>        # fixed by tuning, broken by tuning, still wrong

review sorts every example into fixed by tuning, broken by tuning (the base model had it right), still wrong and still right. Fix or add training examples for what is still wrong, tokenise again, train again and run the same test: the numbers show whether it helped. More in The Bhaskera Dashboard.

docs.title: Step 8: Benchmark Against the Base Model
docs.text:
Training loss does not say what the model can still do. Download the test data once on a login node (compute nodes have no internet), then run the standard tests on the base and the tuned model:

$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.evaluate prepare --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag
$ ./submit.sh eval --run <run id> --tasks arc_easy,hellaswag --limit 200      # --limit: a quick check; leave it out for the real score

The result shows the change per task and counts as better or worse only when it is larger than twice the standard error. It is stored with the run and shown in the Runs table; Compare models puts several side by side. Use the same tests and the same number of examples for every model you compare.

docs.title: Step 9: Save the Model
docs.text:
Give the trained model a name, a version and a note, so a colleague can find it without a run id:

$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.register add --run <run id> --name my-assistant --alias champion
$ python -m bhaskera.launcher.register list

Chat, benchmark and compare accept the registered name in place of a run id (my-assistant, my-assistant:2, my-assistant@champion). On the dashboard this is Register. See Model Registry for versions, aliases and notes. A run that stopped early can be continued with ./submit.sh resume --run <run id> (Resuming a Job).
